AGENCY:
Enforcement and Compliance, International Trade Administration, Department of Commerce.
SUMMARY:
The U.S. Department of Commerce (Commerce) finds that revocation of the countervailing duty (CVD) order on utility scale wind towers (wind towers) from Malaysia would be likely to lead to continuation or recurrence of countervailable subsidies at the levels indicated in the “Final Results of Sunset Review” section of this notice.
DATES:
Applicable November 2, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Connor Field, Office V, Enforcement and Compliance, International Trade Administration, U.S. Department of Commerce, 1401 Constitution Avenue NW, Washington, DC 20230; telephone: 202-482-3997.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Background
On August 4, 2021, Commerce published in the
Federal Register
the CVD order on wind towers from Malaysia.[1]
On July 2, 2026, Commerce published the notice of initiation of the first sunset review of the
Order,
pursuant to section 751(c) of the Tariff Act of 1930, as amended (the Act) and 19 CFR 351.218(c).[2]
On July 17, 2026, Commerce received a notice of intent to participate in this review from the domestic interested party, within the deadline specified in 19 CFR 351.218(d)(1)(i).[3]
The domestic interested party claimed interested party status under sections 771(9)(C) and (F) of the Act as a U.S. producer and as a coalition consisting of a U.S. producer of the domestic like product.[4]
On August 3, 2026, Commerce received an adequate substantive response from the domestic interested party within the 30-day deadline specified in 19 CFR 351.218(d)(3)(i).[5]
Commerce did not receive a substantive response from either the Government of Malaysia or any other respondent interested party to this proceeding. On August 24, 2026, Commerce notified the U.S. International Trade Commission (ITC) that it did not receive an adequate substantive response from respondent interested parties.[6]
As a result, Commerce conducted an expedited (120-day) sunset review of the
Order,
pursuant to section 751(c)(3)(B) of the Act and 19 CFR 351.218(e)(1)(ii)(B)(2) and (C)(2).
Scope of the Order
The products covered by the
Order
are utility scale wind towers. For a full description of the scope,
see
the Issues and Decision Memorandum.[7]
Analysis of Comments Received
A complete discussion of all issues raised in this sunset review, including the likelihood of continuation or recurrence of subsidization and the
( printed page 68494)
countervailable subsidy rates likely to prevail if the
Order
were to be revoked, is contained in the accompanying Issues and Decision Memorandum.[8]
A list of the topics discussed in the Issues and Decision Memorandum is attached as an appendix to this notice. The Issues and Decision Memorandum is a public document and is on file electronically via Enforcement and Compliance's Antidumping and Countervailing Duty Centralized Electronic Service System, which is available to registered users at
https://access.trade.gov.
In addition, a complete version of the Issues and Decision Memorandum can be accessed directly at
https://access.trade.gov/frnotices.
Final Results of Sunset Review
Pursuant to sections 751(c) and 752(b) of the Act, Commerce determines that revocation of the
Order
would be likely to lead to continuation or recurrence of countervailable subsidies at the following net countervailable subsidy rates:

We are issuing and publishing these final results in accordance with sections 751(c), 752(b), and 777(i)(1) of the Act, and 19 CFR 351.221(c)(5)(ii).

articles.title: China’s New Export Controls: Selling the Output, Keeping the Capability - orfonline.org
articles.summary: China’s New Export Controls: Selling the Output, Keeping the Capability  orfonline.org
articles.full_text:
Having moved from imitation to the frontier in AI, biomedicine, and solar, Beijing is now deciding who may follow it there, and India may be among those left waiting
Image Source:  Getty Images  
China is marking its arrival as a technology power in the customary fashion: by deciding who may not have its technology. By joining the United States and other advanced economies in erecting export controls around key technologies, Beijing is signalling that it now has something worth guarding. The legal architecture, too, is being assembled swiftly and in sequence.
On 16 October, the Ministry of Commerce (MOFCOM) and the Ministry of Science and Technology proposed adding AI, biomedicine, and photovoltaic technologies to China’s catalogue of technologies that are prohibited or restricted from export. The proposals are drafts and will be finalised after consultation. Once they are, restricted items will require an export licence, and prohibited items will be barred outright. Exporters will also have to disclose any transfer of covered technology before it takes place, which gives the state a window to intervene and hands it a standing view of who is seeking what.
Three days later, on 19 October, MOFCOM and the General Administration of Customs placed certain tunnel boring machines and their components, dredgers, and specialised excavators designed for use above 3,000 metres under export control. The altitude threshold is the giveaway. Civilian demand for such equipment at that height is slight, except where roads and tunnels are being driven through the Himalayas. India is doing exactly that, building and upgrading infrastructure along the Line of Actual Control (LAC), the de facto border. The measure never names India, but its timing is instructive. The two sides have spent the past year in a cautious thaw, marked by patrolling arrangements, resumed dialogue, and talk of an “early harvest” on the boundary. Beijing is showing that thaw and leverage are not mutually exclusive.
The aim is to stop transfers that could cause the loss of the underlying know-how: the process recipes, the model architectures, the production lines. Beijing is, in effect, trying to keep the capability at home while exporting the output.
The logic behind the technology lists is subtler than that of a simple embargo. The aim is not to block products built with these technologies; Chinese solar panels, drugs, and AI services will continue to sell. The aim is to stop transfers that could cause the loss of the underlying know-how: the process recipes, the model architectures, the production lines. Beijing is, in effect, trying to keep the capability at home while exporting the output.
The regulatory loophole that Beijing is closing was exposed by the Manus affair. Meta was able to acquire the Chinese-founded AI agent app, a transaction that moved valuable technology and talent offshore without tripping any existing export control. Chinese authorities subsequently blocked the deal. The new draft rules are meant to ensure that no future Manus slips through on a technicality.
The wider purpose is to retain control over the technology needed to replicate Chinese industrial capacity abroad, and thereby to bind global supply chains more tightly to China. This is where the measures concern India directly. Countries pursuing a “China+1” strategy, which seek to diversify manufacturing away from China without leaving the Chinese ecosystem entirely, depend on importing not just components but also process knowledge, equipment, and engineers. A factory in India or Vietnam making solar cells or biologics needs more than a purchase order; it needs the know-how. Restrict that, and the “+1” remains a showroom rather than a competitor. India, with its production-linked incentive (PLI) schemes in electronics, solar modules, and pharmaceuticals, is the most obvious casualty.
The AI provisions in the new notifications run to 23 proposed technologies. They cover large models, agents, chip design, computing clusters, and cyber and information-processing capabilities. The proposals are framed around safety and risk, the vocabulary Washington has also adopted for its own restrictions. For now, however, the restrictions target capabilities rather than the riskiest systems, and rules written around capabilities apply to nearly anyone building anything useful.
To promote its World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organisation (WAICO), Beijing proposes additional facilitation and support for technology exports that advance cooperation among members. Membership brings access; non-membership brings paperwork. It is a familiar structure: a club whose benefits are defined partly by what non-members cannot get.
China has acquired the means to monitor, slow, or block the flow of its AI technology whenever it chooses. A licensing regime requires no dramatic announcement, only discretion. Delays can be passed off as bureaucratic, and refusals can be left unexplained.
According to an analysis by Bharat Reddy, nothing changes immediately, “but the basis for leverage exists.” That is the crux of the matter. China has acquired the means to monitor, slow, or block the flow of its AI technology whenever it chooses. A licensing regime requires no dramatic announcement, only discretion. Delays can be passed off as bureaucratic, and refusals can be left unexplained.
For the biomedicine list, five technologies are proposed, covering cell and gene therapies and small interfering RNA (siRNA) drugs. These are high-value fields in which Chinese firms have moved from imitation to the frontier within a decade, and in which licensing deals with Western pharmaceutical companies have multiplied. Control over them lets Beijing decide who gets to commercialise Chinese science.
The photovoltaic list, which contains 12 technologies, is the most consequential for the industry. Production technologies for thin-wafer fluidised-bed polysilicon and for perovskite cells would be prohibited outright, while others, including TOPCon and heterojunction, would need a licence. China dominates every stage of the solar supply chain, and these are the technologies that determine who will make the next generation of cells cheaply. Prohibiting the newest means competitors cannot leapfrog; licensing the rest means they can follow, but only at a pace Beijing approves.
Effectively, Beijing could be curbing exports of solar manufacturing technology to India. Analysts say China is seeking to preserve its dominance as India builds up its domestic manufacturing capabilities and tries to shake off its dependence on China. Earlier this year, New Delhi eased certain rules governing Chinese investment to encourage cooperation between Indian and Chinese companies in areas such as polysilicon and silicon wafer production. The new Chinese regulations, however, will create uncertainty for the planned collaborations.
One provision deserves particular notice. Even an overseas factory built with Chinese equipment may remain within the scope of the controls after the machines are installed. The restriction thus follows the technology across the border and persists after delivery. A plant in India or elsewhere would not simply own its machines; it would operate them under the continuing shadow of Chinese regulatory reach, which would affect upgrades, servicing, and the re-export of what they produce.
The 19 October order also recalibrated drone export controls. Covered items now include unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) that fly beyond natural line of sight with an endurance of three hours or more, or a range of 300 km or more. They also include radios above 30 dBmW or capable of controlling more than 10 aircraft, aerosol dispersal systems above 80 litres, high-power brushless motors, carbon-fibre propellers, and technologies for flight control, autonomous navigation, sense-and-avoid, whole-system design, and counter-UAS operations. Taken together, the list covers nearly every element from which an indigenous drone industry could be assembled, which matters to an India that is trying to build precisely that after the lessons of recent conflicts.
The pattern is unmistakable. Beijing is following Washington’s playbook, and applying it with the advantage of owning the chokepoints in several of the sectors concerned. For India, the message is that diversification away from China will be permitted only on terms that leave China indispensable.
Manoj Joshi is a Distinguished Fellow at the Observer Research Foundation.

articles.title: “China Leans on Exports as the EU Raises Its Defenses”: Trade Tensions Escalate, Fueling Calls for Tougher Measures Including a European Version of Section 301 - https://economy.ac/
articles.summary: “China Leans on Exports as the EU Raises Its Defenses”: Trade Tensions Escalate, Fueling Calls for Tougher Measures Including a European Version of Section 301  https://economy.ac/
articles.full_text:
Authored On
Modified
EU-China trade tensions deepen, spreading to chemicals
Germany and France urge a European version of Section 301 modeled on the U.S. framework
China’s drive to offload excess output abroad compounds Europe’s economic strain, threatening industrial competitiveness
China has launched an anti-dumping investigation into chemicals imported from the European Union (EU). The move follows a series of recent EU trade remedy actions against Chinese chemicals, prompting Beijing to respond in kind. Market observers expect the trade dispute between the two sides could become structurally entrenched and protracted. China’s growing dependence on exports is colliding directly with mounting European concerns over its trade deficit with China and weakening manufacturing competitiveness.
EU and China Exchange Trade Remedy Actions
According to a report by China’s state-run Xinhua News Agency on October 3, with all dates given in local time, China’s Ministry of Commerce announced that day that it had opened an anti-dumping investigation into para-nitrotoluene imported from the EU. Also known as p-nitrotoluene, the substance is a chemical intermediate used in the production of dyes, pharmaceuticals and pesticides. The ministry said the investigation followed a complaint by Chinese para-nitrotoluene producers and was based on preliminary evidence that EU products were being imported at dumped prices, causing injury to domestic producers. Industry data show that prices of EU-origin para-nitrotoluene fell by approximately 60% cumulatively between 2022 and 2025. The ministry’s investigation covers alleged dumping from July last year through June this year and is scheduled to conclude in October next year.
The investigation is widely interpreted as a response to recent EU trade remedy actions. The European Commission opened three anti-dumping investigations last month into chemical products, including imports from China. The products under investigation are polyvinyl chloride (PVC), acetylsalicylic acid and cellulose ethers. Specifically, on September 23, the Commission launched separate investigations into certain PVC imports from China, South Korea, Mexico and Taiwan, and into acetylsalicylic acid from China. On September 24, it opened another investigation into cellulose ethers from China and South Korea. The EU cited industry complaints alleging that these products were entering the bloc’s market at dumped prices and causing injury to European producers.
The Tariff War Between the Two Sides
This is not the first exchange of trade restrictions between the EU and China. In September 2023, for example, the EU announced plans for an anti-subsidy investigation, arguing that low-priced electric vehicles benefiting from Chinese government subsidies were distorting the European market. In October that year, it formally launched an investigation on its own initiative into battery electric vehicles (BEVs) from China. The EU subsequently introduced provisional countervailing duties in July 2024, completed the investigation in October that year and imposed definitive countervailing duties for five years. The final rates included 17.0% for BYD, 18.8% for Geely and 35.3% for SAIC, while Tesla’s China-made vehicles were subject to a rate of 7.8%. These duties are levied in addition to the EU’s existing 10% tariff on cars.
China responded by expanding trade remedy investigations into EU products. In January 2024, China’s Ministry of Commerce launched an anti-dumping investigation into EU brandy, including French cognac. In June that year, it opened an anti-dumping investigation into EU pork and pig by-products, followed in August by an anti-subsidy investigation into certain EU dairy products, including cheese and cream. China subsequently introduced provisional anti-dumping measures in October 2024 requiring deposits of 30.6–39.0% on EU brandy, before issuing a final determination and confirming anti-dumping measures in July last year. EU pork was also subjected to provisional anti-dumping measures of 15.6–62.4% in September last year, followed by a final decision in December to impose anti-dumping duties of 4.9–19.8%. Certain EU dairy products likewise became subject to countervailing duties of 7.4–11.7% for five years following the conclusion of the anti-subsidy investigation this February.
A Head-On Clash in Public Procurement
EU-China trade tensions have also been pronounced in public procurement. In April 2024, the Commission launched an investigation on its own initiative into China’s public procurement market for medical devices. It cited practices by the Chinese government and public institutions that encouraged purchases of domestically produced equipment or imposed unfavorable conditions on imported products during tendering, restricting European companies’ market access. According to findings released by the Commission in January last year, approximately 87% of the Chinese medical device procurement tenders examined contained conditions excluding or discriminating against imported equipment. The EU said consultations with China had failed to produce an agreement on opening the market and finalized restrictions in June last year. As a result, Chinese companies were generally barred from bidding for EU medical device procurement contracts worth approximately $5.60 million or more. Even where a non-Chinese company won a contract, medical devices originating in China could account for no more than 50% of its total value.
China’s Ministry of Finance retaliated by excluding EU companies from medical device government procurement projects with budgets of approximately $6.71 million or more from July last year. EU companies are excluded from bidding for these projects regardless of their products’ origin, while medical devices imported from the EU must account for less than 50% of the contract value when a non-EU company submits a bid. However, European-owned companies manufacturing products locally in China were exempted from the restrictions, as were cases in which only EU products could meet procurement requirements. China’s Ministry of Commerce publicly described the policy as a “reciprocal restrictive measure” responding to the EU’s medical device procurement restrictions.
Table 1. Key Fronts in the EU-China Trade Dispute
| Sector | EU Measures | China’s Response | 
|---|---|---|
| Chemicals | Launched anti-dumping investigations into Chinese polyvinyl chloride, acetylsalicylic acid, cellulose ethers and other products | Launched an anti-dumping investigation into EU-origin para-nitrotoluene | 
| Automobiles and Agricultural Products | Imposed definitive countervailing duties on Chinese electric vehicles | Imposed anti-dumping and countervailing duties on EU brandy, pork and dairy products | 
| Medical Device Procurement | Restricted Chinese companies’ participation and the share of Chinese-origin products in public procurement contracts above a specified threshold | Restricted EU companies’ participation in major government procurement projects and the share of European-origin products | 
| Trade Policy Framework | France and Germany proposed a European version of Section 301 of the U.S. Trade Act to respond swiftly to structurally unfair trade practices | Opposed the proposal as unilateralist and protectionist | 
Calls for a Tougher European Response
As the trade dispute drags on, Europe has recently stepped up efforts to counter China. On October 5, for example, Germany and France released a joint non-paper on responding to the expansion of low-priced Chinese exports and supply chain dependence. They urged the Commission to develop a new instrument capable of restricting third countries’ access to the single market more swiftly and forcefully than existing trade remedy mechanisms. Although the document did not explicitly name any country, it identified an oversupply of Chinese products and heavy dependence on critical raw materials and components as central concerns, leading observers to view the proposal as effectively targeting China.
The framework under discussion resembles Section 301 of the U.S. Trade Act. Section 301 authorizes the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative (USTR) to investigate unfair or discriminatory trade practices by foreign governments and, at the president’s direction, take action such as imposing tariffs or restricting market access. The so-called “European Section 301” envisaged by France and Germany similarly focuses on enabling the EU to act swiftly against broader structural issues, including Chinese industrial subsidies and restricted market access, rather than conducting separate anti-dumping or anti-subsidy investigations into individual products. China, however, has warned that the proposal is unilateralist and protectionist and could undermine China-EU trade and the stability of global supply chains.
The Heavy Economic Toll of the China Shock
Behind the escalating trade confrontation lies China’s deepening dependence on exports. As the property downturn erodes household wealth and domestic demand while deflationary pressures persist, the Chinese government is sustaining economic growth by expanding manufacturing output and exports. According to Bloomberg’s calculations published on September 30, based on data from China’s General Administration of Customs, Chinese exports totaled $2.92 trillion in the first eight months of this year. If that growth trajectory continues, annual exports are projected to reach $4.48 trillion, approximately 80% above their 2019 level.
China’s export strategy has dealt a direct blow to Europe. Eurostat data show that last year the EU exported approximately $223.63 billion in goods to China and imported approximately $626.75 billion, leaving a trade deficit of approximately $403.12 billion. articles.full_text:
Toyota Motor Corporation
World's largest automaker by volume
Japan recorded a trade deficit of about 556.5 billion yen in September 2026, as imports outpaced exports, according to the country's trade statistics released on October 29, 2026. The figures, published by Japan Customs, show exports rose 16.5 percent from September 2025 to roughly 10.95 trillion yen, while imports climbed 18.9 percent to about 11.51 trillion yen.
Exports to Asia totaled about 6.07 trillion yen, up 17.3 percent year on year, while imports from the region reached roughly 6.03 trillion yen, up 22.2 percent, leaving a small surplus. Shipments to China fell to about 1.73 trillion yen, a gain of 8.5 percent, but imports from China rose 16.4 percent to about 2.76 trillion yen, producing a deficit of roughly 1.03 trillion yen.
Exports to the United States increased 22.9 percent to about 1.96 trillion yen, while imports from the United States rose 44.8 percent to about 1.57 trillion yen, leaving a surplus of roughly 391.7 billion yen. Exports to the European Union grew 10.4 percent to about 984.3 billion yen, and imports from the bloc were nearly flat, edging down 0.1 percent to about 1.13 trillion yen.
Transport equipment was the largest export category at about 2.28 trillion yen, up 10.8 percent, followed by electrical machinery at about 2.15 trillion yen, up 30.2 percent, and machinery at about 1.95 trillion yen, up 18.2 percent. Within electrical machinery, semiconductor exports rose 49.4 percent to about 933.6 billion yen.
On the import side, mineral fuels were the largest category at about 2.35 trillion yen, up 39.4 percent, with petroleum imports rising 51.1 percent to about 1.11 trillion yen. Electrical machinery imports totaled about 2.13 trillion yen, up 23.4 percent, and machinery imports reached about 1.26 trillion yen, up 27.0 percent.

Japan recorded a trade deficit in August 2026, with exports valued at about 10.04 trillion yen against imports of roughly 11.16 trillion yen, according to detailed trade statistics released by Japan Customs. The figures, published on October 29, 2026, show exports rising 19.3 percent from August 2025, while imports climbed 28.1 percent, leaving a shortfall of approximately 1.12 trillion yen.
Exports to Asia totaled about 5.75 trillion yen, up 21.3 percent year on year, while imports from the region reached some 5.43 trillion yen, a gain of 29.2 percent, producing a surplus of roughly 319 billion yen. Shipments to China were about 1.81 trillion yen, up 20.5 percent, but imports from China rose 22.6 percent to around 2.36 trillion yen, resulting in a deficit of some 553 billion yen.
Exports to the United States amounted to about 1.72 trillion yen, an increase of 24.9 percent, and imports from the United States were roughly 1.66 trillion yen, up 55.3 percent, leaving a surplus of about 69 billion yen. Trade with the European Union showed exports of some 866 billion yen, up 11.0 percent, and imports of about 1.10 trillion yen, up 20.4 percent, for a deficit of roughly 231 billion yen.
Exports to the Middle East fell 5.2 percent to about 283 billion yen, while imports from the region declined 4.2 percent to some 869 billion yen, yielding a deficit of about 585 billion yen.
Among export categories worldwide, electrical machinery was valued at about 2.00 trillion yen, up 31.5 percent, and transport equipment at some 1.82 trillion yen, up 7.9 percent. Machinery exports totaled roughly 1.77 trillion yen, a rise of 20.9 percent.
On the import side, mineral fuels were the largest category at about 2.47 trillion yen, up 38.5 percent, followed by electrical machinery at some 1.90 trillion yen, up 41.1 percent, and machinery at about 1.23 trillion yen, up 35.1 percent.

articles.title: India's trade deficit to persist amid oil import dependence, petroleum exports offer relief: IIFT VC - www.indiagazette.com
articles.summary: India's trade deficit to persist amid oil import dependence, petroleum exports offer relief: IIFT VC  www.indiagazette.com
articles.full_text:
ANI
                
30 Oct 2026, 23:03 GMT+10
            
New Delhi [India], October 30 (ANI): India's trade deficit is likely to persist as long as the country remains dependent on oil imports, although rising exports of value-added petroleum products are helping narrow the gap, K. Rangarajan, Vice-Chancellor of the Indian Institute of Foreign Trade (IIFT), said on Friday.
"Trade deficit will continue to be there till the time we have more and more dependence on oil. It cannot be reduced, but it is getting somewhat reduced because of those value addition," Rangarajan told ANI in an exclusive interview.
Explaining the factors behind India's trade deficit, he said the country's dependence on imported oil remained a structural challenge.
However, India has emerged as an important destination for refining and exporting value-added petroleum products, particularly following disruptions caused by the war and the Middle East crisis. Refining activities and subsequent exports were helping partly offset the impact of oil imports, he added.
On India's foreign trade outlook for FY27, Rangarajan expressed optimism about the country's ability to surpass the USD 1 trillion export milestone, citing a more conducive environment for external engagements.
"I am also very optimistic about it. We will be able to surpass that $1 trillion as well. So, it should not be a surprise," he said, adding that his optimism was based on the emerging global trade landscape.
On the broader economic outlook, he estimated that India's growth rate could reach around 6-7 per cent, supported by expanding external engagements and changing geopolitical dynamics.
Highlighting the challenges facing the manufacturing sector, Rangarajan said government policy announcements and industry-friendly interventions alone would not be sufficient to improve competitiveness.
Their effective implementation at the ground level, including by state governments, and the industry's ability to adapt to changing trade conditions would be equally important, he said.
He said businesses needed to understand the implications of free trade agreements (FTAs), including product-specific tariff concessions, tariff lines and rules of origin, rather than leaving such assessments entirely to policymakers.
Describing India's new-generation FTAs as more comprehensive, he said they were no longer limited to tariff reductions but also covered supply chains and services. The industry needed to adapt to these integrated arrangements to translate market access into higher exports.
Citing the India-UAE trade agreement, he said exports had started increasing following its implementation. He expressed optimism about the benefits of other agreements, including the India-New Zealand FTA, while indicating that the European Union agreement could also be implemented and an arrangement with the United States was on the horizon.
On concerns over US President Donald Trump's tariff policies, Rangarajan said frequent changes, additional conditions and uncertainty surrounding tariffs could eventually put pressure on the US market itself.
"The market and its tolerance make a difference," he said, pointing out that China continued to emerge as a major exporter to the US despite the imposition of tariffs as high as 100 per cent.
On foreign investment, he said India needed greater inflows into technology and digital sectors to strengthen its ambition of becoming a global manufacturing hub.
At the same time, overseas investments by Indian companies were increasingly becoming strategic, allowing businesses to explore alternative production and export destinations amid tariff-related uncertainties.
Addressing geopolitical disruptions in West Asia, including concerns surrounding the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea, he said India was relatively better positioned because of its diplomatic relationships with various countries.
He noted that global trade was estimated to grow by around 1 per cent, while growth in the ASEAN region and India was projected to exceed 2 per cent.
Rangarajan said India's diplomatic engagement had helped it navigate disruptions during the Russia-Ukraine conflict and other international crises. He also expressed confidence that India could contribute to rebuilding countries affected by wars and infrastructure destruction.
"Whenever there are problems in other countries, India is the first country to help, be it in our neighbour Nepal or somewhere in Africa," he said, adding that India could play a significant role in supporting reconstruction efforts while strengthening its own trade prospects. (ANI)

articles.title: Rebalancing India’s trade deficits - EY
articles.summary: Rebalancing India’s trade deficits  EY
articles.full_text:
EY refers to the global organization, and may refer to one or more, of the member firms of Ernst & Young Global Limited, each of which is a separate legal entity. Ernst & Young Global Limited, a UK company limited by guarantee, does not provide services to clients.
India's expanding network of bilateral and regional trade agreements offers another channel. Existing agreements and those signed, concluded or awaiting implementation can be used to diversify markets, improve market access and widen the country's export base. Local-currency settlement may complement this strategy where trade flows are sufficiently balanced and the required financial infrastructure is available. It cannot, however, substitute for export competitiveness or supply-chain resilience.
A country-specific rebalancing strategy may also be useful. Illustrative calibrations show how trade could expand while reducing unusually large bilateral imbalances. For the US, considering a scenario in which India's goods and services exports grow at 10% annually while imports grow at about 16%, India’s bilateral trade with the US increases to close to US$500 billion by 2031 while reducing India's present goods-and-services surplus to nearly half its 2025 level. This may be viewed as an illustrative medium-term rebalancing pathway rather than a forecast.
The strategic objective may therefore be to improve the composition and resilience of India's trade rather than mechanically eliminate deficits. Diversifying markets and supply chains, increasing domestic value addition, exploiting opportunities arising from BRICS+ and India's trade agreements, and developing higher-value exports can all contribute to this transition. Over time, a healthier balance with major trading partners, accompanied by an expanding overall volume of trade, would reduce external vulnerabilities while allowing India to retain access to energy, technology and other productive imports essential for growth.

articles.full_text:
Toyota Motor Corporation
World's largest automaker by volume
Japan recorded a trade deficit of 2,847,078 million yen for the April-September period of fiscal 2026, according to trade statistics published by Japan Customs. The figures, released on October 29, 2026, show exports of 63,438,551 million yen against imports of 66,285,629 million yen, with exports rising 18.3 percent and imports climbing 20.5 percent on a year-on-year basis.
The latest deficit figure carries a year-on-year change of 100.8 percent. For the full fiscal year 2025, exports totaled 113,220,318 million yen and imports 114,978,288 million yen, producing a deficit of 1,757,970 million yen.
Within the six-month period, the April-June quarter produced exports of 30,932,054 million yen, up 17.0 percent, and imports of 31,457,095 million yen, up 15.9 percent, leaving a deficit of 525,041 million yen. The July-September quarter showed exports of 32,506,497 million yen, up 19.6 percent, and imports of 34,828,534 million yen, up 24.8 percent, widening the quarterly deficit to 2,322,037 million yen.
On a monthly basis, September recorded exports of 10,953,854 million yen, up 16.5 percent, and imports of 11,510,333 million yen, up 18.9 percent, for a deficit of 556,479 million yen. August showed the largest monthly gap in the period, with exports of 10,043,270 million yen and imports of 11,163,907 million yen producing a deficit of 1,120,637 million yen.
Exports to Asia totaled 35,325,385 million yen, up 20.2 percent, while imports from the region reached 33,951,691 million yen, up 26.2 percent, yielding a surplus of 1,373,694 million yen. Trade with China recorded exports of 10,892,903 million yen and imports of 15,496,741 million yen, a deficit of 4,603,838 million yen.
Exports to the United States amounted to 11,331,909 million yen, up 17.2 percent, and imports from the United States totaled 9,211,168 million yen, up 43.9 percent, producing a surplus of 2,120,741 million yen. Trade with the European Union showed exports of 5,791,845 million yen and imports of 6,641,943 million yen, a deficit of 850,098 million yen.
Exports to the Middle East fell 16.6 percent to 1,698,509 million yen, while imports from the region declined 18.8 percent to 4,401,797 million yen, leaving a deficit of 2,703,288 million yen. Trade with Russia recorded exports of 234,435 million yen and imports of 436,559 million yen.
Transport equipment was the largest export category at 12,989,968 million yen, accounting for 20.5 percent of total exports, followed by electrical machinery at 11,898,211 million yen and machinery at 11,029,218 million yen. Within electrical machinery, semiconductors reached 4,905,368 million yen, up 50.8 percent.
On the import side, mineral fuels were the largest category at 12,748,408 million yen, or 19.2 percent of total imports, followed by electrical machinery at 11,703,538 million yen and machinery at 7,368,451 million yen. Imports of foodstuff totaled 5,473,626 million yen.

articles.title: Fed holds interest rates steady in last decision before midterms
articles.summary: Fed chair Kevin Warsh said politics played no role in pause of interest rate hikes, despite inflation remaining above 3%The US Federal Reserve left interest rates unchanged on Wednesday during its last board meeting before the midterm elections, keeping rates at one of the highest pre-election levels seen in over 20 years.Two out of 12 board members voted against the pause, preferring to raise rates by a quarter point this meeting, the Fed board said in a statement. Continue reading...
articles.full_text:
The US Federal Reserve left interest rates unchanged on Wednesday during its last board meeting before the midterm elections, keeping rates at one of the highest pre-election levels seen in over 20 years.
Two out of 12 board members voted against the pause, preferring to raise rates by a quarter point this meeting, the Fed board said in a statement.
Last month, Fed officials raised rates for the first time since 2023, citing rising inflation, bringing rates to a range of 3.75% to 4%. Inflation has hovered for years above the Fed’s target rate of 2%, and for most of this year, the annualized inflation rate has remained above 3%.
Though inflation rose higher in September, going from 3.4% in August to 3.7%, the pause signals the central bank is taking a wait-and-see approach ahead of the midterms next week.
During a press conference on Wednesday afternoon, the Fed chair, Kevin Warsh, told reporters that the upcoming election played no role in deliberations.
“Politics played no role in the decision,” he said. “I didn’t hear an utterance about politics.”
The central bank is still focused on price stability, he said, but emphasized that “the information that we receive over the coming period will help us determine where want policy to be”.
“The period right in front of us is information rich, there’s a lot that’s happening in the world, my colleagues and I are keen to take notice of it,” he said.
September’s rate hike infuriated Donald Trump, who said that “interest rates in the United States should be 1% or less”.
Warsh declined to comment on a remark from Donald Trump that, besides Warsh, the Fed board is full of Democratic-appointed members who “would like to see the country do badly”, but said that the latest meeting was “a heck of a family fight”.
“I’m honored to be here, and I’m honored to be chairman of this group,” he said.
Interest rates determine the cost of interest for loans, including for credit cards, mortgage and some savings accounts. During times of high inflation, raising rates can slow price increases.
Multiple Fed leaders have suggested in recent weeks that the central bank has room for a pause, even if most Fed economists are predicting one more rate hike before the end of the year.
“The hikes do not need to come at consecutive meetings, but they should be in place in an acceptable period of time,” the Fed governor Christopher Waller said earlier this month.
The proximity of the election also made it more likely that the Fed will “not take any radical action”, said Nicholas Economides, a professor of economics at the NYU Stern Business School.
“Even if the Fed were to do something radically different, the economy would not have time to adjust before the elections,” he said.
Rising prices this year have largely been driven by war in the Middle East with Iran. Oil prices have soared with the closure of the strait of Hormuz, a crucial passageway for trade. Inflation rose last month to its highest level since the spring, while oil traded briefly above $117 a barrel earlier this week, its highest price in more than six months.
The higher cost of living is expected to play a crucial role in the upcoming midterm elections that will determine which party will control Congress. Across multiple polls, the economy has been cited as the top issue for voters.
By itself, hiking interest rates cannot solely address inflation caused by supply shocks, Economides said. Raising rates is helpful for when the economy is too hot, or when demand outpaces supply, but can be counterproductive otherwise.
“If inflation is caused by supply factors, it doesn’t make sense to try to cure it by increasing interest rates because it won’t work,” he said. “It will slow down the economy at a time in which you don’t want it to slow down.
On Wednesday, Warsh also announced upcoming changes to the Fed’s eight board meetings it conducts annually. Starting in fall 2027, only seven of those meetings will be convened to set interest rates. That number will go down to six in 2028, with the other meetings dedicated to “broad monetary policy” when the change is implemented.

articles.full_text:
This document amends the Table of TV Allotments (table) of the Federal Communications Commission's (Commission) rules by substituting VHF channel 10 for UHF channel 20 at Elko, Nevada in response to a petition for rulemaking filed by Reno (KENV-TV) Licensee, Inc.
(Licensee), the licensee of full power television station KENV-DT (KENV-DT or Station), Elko, Nevada.
The Media Bureau (Bureau) previously granted a petition for rulemaking submitted by the Licensee to substitute UHF channel 20 for VHF channel 10 at Elko in the table, and subsequently granted a construction permit for its new channel.
The Licensee states that it was unable to complete construction of the channel 20 facility by the deadline specified in the Station's construction permit.
The Licensee filed the instant petition to amend the table to substitute VHF channel 10 for UHF channel 20 and allow KENV-DT to continue to operate on channel 10 at its licensed parameters and provide uninterrupted service to viewers.
The staff engineering analysis finds that the proposal is in compliance with the Commission's principal community coverage and technical requirements, including the interference protection requirements.
In support of its channel substitution request, the Licensee filed comments reaffirming its interest and stating that it commits to promptly take any and all steps that may be necessary to effectuate the channel substitution proposed in the petition.
An individual commenter, Steven Quinn Singleton, also filed comments, which, for the reasons discussed in the Report and Order referenced below, the Bureau denied.

Published Document: 2026-22007 (91 FR 67782)
This document has been published in the Federal Register. Use the PDF linked in the document sidebar for the official electronic format.
AGENCY:
National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS), National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), Commerce.
ACTION:
Temporary rule; quota transfer.
SUMMARY:
NMFS announces that the State of New York is transferring a portion of their 2026 commercial bluefish quota to the State of North Carolina. This quota adjustment is necessary to comply with the Atlantic Bluefish Fishery Management Plan (FMP) quota transfer provisions. This announcement informs the public of the revised 2026 commercial bluefish quotas for New York and North Carolina.
DATES:
Effective October 27, 2026 through December 31, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Matthew Rigdon, Fishery Management Specialist, (978) 281-9336.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Regulations governing the Atlantic bluefish fishery are found in 50 CFR 648.160 through 648.167. These regulations require annual specification of a commercial quota that is apportioned among the coastal states from Maine through Florida. The process to set the annual commercial quota and the percent allocated to each state is described in § 648.162, and the final 2026 allocations were published on February 19, 2026 (91 FR 7896).
The final rule implementing amendment 1 to the FMP, as published in the
Federal Register
on July 26, 2000 (65 FR 45844), provided a mechanism for transferring bluefish commercial quota from one state to another. Two or more states, under mutual agreement and with the concurrence of the NMFS Greater Atlantic Regional Administrator, can request approval to transfer or combine bluefish commercial quota under § 648.162(e). The Regional Administrator is required to consider three criteria in the evaluation of requests for quota transfers or combinations: (1) the transfers would not preclude the overall annual quota from being fully harvested; (2) the transfers address an unforeseen variation or contingency in the fishery; and (3) the transfers are consistent with the objectives of the FMP and the Magnuson-Stevens Fishery Conservation and Management Act (Magnuson-Stevens Act). The Regional Administrator has determined these criteria have been met for the transfers approved in this notification.
New York is transferring 200,000 pounds (lb) (90,718 kilograms (kg)) of Atlantic bluefish to North Carolina through mutual agreement of the states. This transfer was requested to ensure North Carolina would not exceed its 2026 state quota. The revised bluefish quotas for 2026 are: New York, 596,248 lb (270,454 kg); and North Carolina, 1,943,521 lb (881,566 kg).
( printed page 67783)
Classification
NMFS issues this action pursuant to section 305(d) of the Magnuson-Stevens Act. This action is required by 50 CFR 648.162(e)(1)(i) through (iii), which was issued pursuant to section 304(b), and is exempted from review under Executive Order 12866.

AGENCY:
National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS), National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), Commerce.
ACTION:
Temporary rule; quota transfer.
SUMMARY:
NMFS announces that the Commonwealth of Virginia is transferring a portion of its 2026 commercial summer flounder quota to the State of New Jersey. This adjustment to the 2026 fishing year quota is necessary to comply with the Summer Flounder, Scup, and Black Sea Bass Fishery Management Plan (FMP) quota transfer provisions. This announcement informs the public of the revised 2026 commercial quotas for Virginia and New Jersey.
DATES:
Effective October 27, 2026, through December 31, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Matthew Rigdon, Fishery Management Specialist, (978) 281-9336.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Regulations governing the summer flounder fishery are found in 50 CFR 648.100 through 648.111. These regulations require annual specification of a commercial quota that is apportioned among the coastal states from Maine through North Carolina. The process to set the annual commercial quota and the percent allocated to each state is described in § 648.102, and the final 2026 allocations were published on February 19, 2026 (91 FR 7896).
The final rule implementing amendment 5 to the FMP, as published in the
Federal Register
on December 17, 1993 (58 FR 65936), provided a mechanism for transferring summer flounder commercial quota from one state to another. Two or more states, under mutual agreement and with the concurrence of the NMFS Greater Atlantic Regional Administrator, can transfer or combine summer flounder commercial quota under § 648.102(c)(2). The Regional Administrator is required to consider three criteria in the evaluation of requests for quota transfers or combinations: (1) the transfers or combinations would not preclude the overall annual quota from being fully harvested; (2) the transfers address an unforeseen variation or contingency in the fishery; and (3) the transfers are consistent with the objectives of the FMP and the Magnuson-Stevens Fishery Conservation and Management Act (Magnuson-Stevens Act). The Regional Administrator has determined that these three criteria have been met for the transfer approved in this notification.
Virginia is transferring 9,745 pounds (lb; 4,420 kilograms (kg)) of summer flounder to New Jersey through a mutual agreement between the states. This transfer was requested to repay landings made by an out-of-state permitted vessel under a safe harbor agreement. The revised summer flounder quotas for 2026 are: Virginia, 2,423,982 lb (1,099,500 kg); and New Jersey, 2,119,613 lb (961,440 kg).
Classification
NMFS issues this action pursuant to section 305(d) of the Magnuson-Stevens Act. This action is required by 50 CFR 648.102(c)(2)(i) through (iv), which was issued pursuant to section 304(b) of the Magnuson-Stevens Act, and is exempted from review under Executive Order 12866.

Published Document: 2026-21997 (91 FR 67765)
This document has been published in the Federal Register. Use the PDF linked in the document sidebar for the official electronic format.
( printed page 67765)
AGENCY:
Office of Government Ethics.
ACTION:
Final rule; technical amendments.
SUMMARY:
The U.S. Office of Government Ethics (OGE) is updating its executive branch regulation on financial disclosure to reflect the retroactive statutory increase of the reporting thresholds for gifts and travel reimbursements. OGE is also updating the executive branchwide standards of ethical conduct regulation to raise the widely attended gatherings nonsponsor gifts exception dollar ceiling tied to these thresholds. This latter change is not retroactive.
DATES:
Effective date:
This final rule is effective October 28, 2026.
Applicability date:
The amendments to 5 CFR 2634.304 and 2634.907 are applicable as of January 1, 2026.
The U.S. Office of Government Ethics (OGE) is amending pertinent sections of its executive branchwide ethics regulations on financial disclosure and standards of ethical conduct, as codified at 5 CFR parts 2634 and 2635, in order to update the thresholds for gifts and travel reimbursements, as well as the widely attended gatherings nonsponsor gifts exception dollar ceiling.
Increased Gifts and Travel Reimbursements Reporting Thresholds
First, OGE is revising its executive branch financial disclosure regulation at 5 CFR part 2634 to reflect the increased reporting thresholds for gifts, reimbursements, and travel expenses for both the public and confidential executive branch financial disclosure systems. The increased thresholds are applicable as of January 1, 2026. These increases conform to the statutorily mandated public disclosure reporting thresholds under the Ethics in Government Act as amended, 5 U.S.C. 13104(a)(2)(A) and (B), and are extended to confidential disclosure reporting by OGE's regulation. Under the Ethics in Government Act, the gifts and travel reimbursements reporting thresholds are tied to the dollar amount for the “minimal value” threshold for foreign gifts as the General Services Administration (GSA) periodically redefines it.
GSA raised the “minimal value” amount under the Foreign Gifts and Decorations Act, 5 U.S.C. 7342, to $525 for the three-year period 2026-2028 (from the prior level of $480) in a December 29, 2025, Federal Management Regulation Bulletin. See Gen. Servs. Admin., GSA Bull. FMR B-2025-01, Foreign Gifts and Decorations Minimal Value (2025) (revising, effective January 1, 2026, the foreign gifts minimal value definition as codified at 41 CFR 102-42.10).
Accordingly, applicable as of January 1, 2026, OGE is increasing the thresholds for reporting of gifts and travel reimbursements from any one source in 5 CFR 2634.304 and 2634.907(g). The thresholds have been raised to “more than $525” for the gifts and travel reimbursements aggregation thresholds and “$210 or less” for the de minimis exception for gifts and travel reimbursements that do not have to be aggregated. As noted, these regulatory increases implement the underlying statutory increases effective January 1, 2026. OGE is also updating the examples following those sections, including appropriate adjustments to gift values.
OGE will continue to adjust the gifts and travel reimbursements reporting thresholds in its part 2634 regulation in the future as needed in light of GSA's redefinition of “minimal value” every three years for foreign gifts purposes. See OGE's prior three-year adjustment of those regulatory reporting thresholds, as published at 88 FR 37753 (June 9, 2023) (for 2023-2025, the aggregate reporting thresholds were more than $480, with a $192 or less de minimis exception).
Increased Dollar Ceiling for the Exception for Nonsponsor Gifts of Free Attendance at Widely Attended Gatherings
OGE is also increasing the exception ceiling for nonsponsor gifts of free attendance at widely attended gatherings from $480 to $525 in the executive branch standards of ethical conduct regulation, as codified at 5 CFR 2635.204(g)(3) (and as illustrated in the examples following paragraph (g)). This separate regulatory change is effective upon publication in the
Federal Register
, on October 28, 2026. As OGE noted in the preambles to the proposed and final rules on such nonsponsor gifts, that ceiling is tied to the financial disclosure gifts reporting threshold. See 60 FR 31415 (June 15, 1995) and 61 FR 42965 (Aug. 20, 1996). Thus, OGE is again increasing the nonsponsor gift ceiling to match the further increase in the gifts and travel reimbursements reporting thresholds described above. The nonsponsor gift ceiling was last raised in June 2023. See 88 FR 37753 (June 9, 2023). The other requirements for acceptance of such nonsponsor gifts, including an agency interest determination and expected attendance by more than 100 persons, remain unchanged.
II. Other Technical Changes
Designation of Notes and Examples
OGE is designating various notes and examples in §§ 2634.304 and 2634.907. The designation of those notes and examples are technical amendments involving no substantive changes to the regulations.
III. Matters of Regulatory Procedure
Administrative Procedure Act
Pursuant to 5 U.S.C. 553(b)(A) and (B), as Acting Director of the Office of Government Ethics, I find that good cause exists for waiving the general notice of proposed rulemaking and public comment procedures as to these technical amendments. The notice and comment procedures are being waived because these amendments concern
( printed page 67766)
matters of agency organization, procedure, and practice. Further, notice and comment is unnecessary because these are technical amendments unlikely to be of significant interest to the public. Finally, it is also in the public interest that the accurate and up-to-date information be contained in the affected sections of OGE's regulations as soon as possible. The increase in the reporting thresholds for gifts and reimbursements is based on a statutory formula and lessens the reporting burden. Therefore, that regulatory revision is retroactively applicable as of January 1, 2026, when the change became effective under the Ethics in Government Act. For the reasons described above, this rule may take immediate effect pursuant to 5 U.S.C. 553(d)(1) and (d)(3).

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Authority for This Rulemaking
The FAA's authority to issue rules regarding aviation safety is found in Title 49 of the United States Code. Subtitle I, Section 106 describes the authority of the FAA Administrator. Subtitle VII, Aviation Programs, describes in more detail the scope of the agency's authority. This rulemaking is promulgated under the authority described in Subtitle VII, Part A, Subpart I, Section 40103. Under that section, the FAA is charged with prescribing regulations to assign the use of the airspace necessary to ensure the safety of aircraft and the efficient use of airspace. This regulation is within the scope of that authority as it modifies Class E airspace to support IFR operations at Samaritan North Lincoln Hospital Heliport, Lincoln City, OR.
History
The FAA published an NPRM for Docket No. FAA-2026-5064 in the
Federal Register
(91 FR 47156; July 28, 2026), modifying the Class E airspace area at Samaritan North Lincoln Hospital Heliport, Lincoln City, OR. Interested parties were invited to participate in this rulemaking effort by submitting written comments on the proposal to the FAA. The FAA received three comments and provides the following responses.
One comment opposed the modification on the basis that it converts uncontrolled airspace to controlled airspace to support private instrument procedures, benefiting commercial enterprises over general aviation. The commenter requested that the FAA “reconsider or narrow this amendment”. Although FAA attempts to preserve navigable airspace to the maximum extent possible, its internal policies require it to designate Class E airspace to accommodate arriving IFR operations.
Another comment suggested an administrative correction to the city name to read, “Lincoln City, OR.” The FAA has made that correction.
The final comment was in support of the modification, but requested additional information regarding the FAA's compliance with the National Environmental Policy Act, which is also discussed in the “Environmental Review” section of this document. However, in response to this commenter's questions, the FAA determined that this action qualifies for categorical exclusion under the National Environmental Policy Act (42 U.S.C. 4321,
et seq.) and in accordance with FAA Order 1050.1G, “FAA National Environmental Policy Act Implementing Procedures,” paragraph B-2.5.a, which applies to “[r]ulemaking actions that designate or modify classes of airspace areas, airways, routes, and reporting points”. In compliance with FAA Order 1050.1G, the FAA reviewed this action for factors and circumstances in which a normally categorically-excluded action may have a significant environmental impact requiring further analysis. It determined that no such extraordinary circumstances exist. The FAA also assessed the potential for impacts to coastal areas or protected-species habitat and determined the impacts would be negligible or non-existent. The FAA also assessed the need for coordination under the Coastal Zone Management Act and found that no such coordination is required. This is an air traffic action, which does not involve land acquisition, physical
( printed page 67769)
ground disturbance, construction, excavation, development activities, or discharges to water bodies.
Incorporation by Reference
Class E airspace designations are published in paragraph 6005 of FAA Order JO 7400.11, Airspace Designations and Reporting Points, which is incorporated by reference in 14 CFR 71.1 on an annual basis. This document amends the current version of that order, FAA Order JO 7400.11M, dated July 30, 2026, and effective September 15, 2026. These amendments will be published in the next update to FAA Order JO 7400.11. FAA Order JO 7400.11M, which lists Class A, B, C, D, and E airspace areas, air traffic service routes, and reporting points, is publicly available as listed in the
ADDRESSES
section of this document.

This action amends 14 CFR part 71 by modifying a Class E airspace area extending upward from 700 feet above the surface at the Samaritan North Lincoln Hospital Heliport, Lincoln City, OR, to contain private-use special instrument flight procedures in support of passenger shuttle, medevac, and cargo operations.

articles.full_text: The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) is publishing a final rule to update the incorporation by reference of several voluntary consensus standards in the Agency's formaldehyde standards for composite wood products regulations under the Toxic Substances Control Act (TSCA) due to the standards having been updated or superseded by the issuing organizations. These new standards primarily update test methods and product standards concerning composite wood products that use formaldehyde. EPA is also conforming these updated standards in the scope and definitional sections in the final rule and incorporating by reference a new small scale quality control chamber test method, similar to current methods already incorporated by reference. EPA is also removing one standard that was previously incorporated by reference to avoid redundancy, given that another identical, internationally recognized version of the standard is already incorporated by reference in this rule.

AGENCY:
Office of the National Coordinator for Health Information Technology (ONC), Department of Health and Human Services (HHS).
ACTION:
Final rule.
SUMMARY:
This final rule focuses on deregulatory actions identified in HHS regulations regarding health information technology standards, implementation specifications, and certification criteria and regarding certification programs for health information technology. This final rule reduces burden, offers flexibility to both developers and providers, and supports innovation through the removal and revision of certain certification criteria and regulatory provisions.
DATES:
This final rule is effective on December 28, 2026, except for amendatory instructions 7, 10, and 12 which are effective January 1, 2027. The incorporation by reference of certain material listed in the rule was approved by the Director of the Federal Register between February 12, 2010, and October 1, 2025.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Michael Lipinski, Office of Programs and Implementation, Office of the National Coordinator for Health Information Technology, 202-690-7151.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Table of Contents
I. Executive Summary
A. Purpose of Deregulatory Action
B. Summary of Major Provisions
1. Health Information Technology Standards, Implementation Specifications, and Certification Criteria and Certification Programs for Health Information Technology (Part 170)
a. Certification Criteria for Health Information Technology
b. Standards and Implementation Specifications for Health Information Technology
c. Terms and Definitions
d. Conditions and Maintenance of Certification Requirements for Health IT Developers
e. ONC Health IT Certification Program Administrative Requirements
C. Severability
D. Costs and Benefits
II. Background
A. Statutory Basis
1. Standards, Implementation Specifications, and Certification Criteria
2. Health IT Certification Program(s)
B. ONC Health IT Certification Program Regulatory History
C. General Comments on the Proposed Rule
D. Comments Beyond the Scope of Certification Program Proposals
III. Health Information Technology Standards, Implementation Specifications, and Certification Criteria and Certification Programs for Health Information Technology (Part 170)
A. Certification Criteria for Health Information Technology
1. Clinical Certification Criteria
a. Clinical Decision Support
b. Family Health History
c. Implantable Device List
2. Care Coordination Certification Criteria
a. Transitions of Care
b. Clinical Information Reconciliation and Incorporation
Since the inception of the ONC Health IT Certification Program (Certification Program) (42 U.S.C. 300jj-11(c)(5)), ONC has aimed to implement and administer the Certification Program in the least burdensome manner that supports an administration's policy goals. Throughout the years, we have worked to improve the Certification Program with a focus on ways to reduce burden, offer flexibility to both developers and providers, and support innovation. Over the past 15 years, we have established a set of regulatory requirements that have provided a foundation for our voluntary Certification Program. As we look to the future, we reviewed the existing requirements and made updates. Through both formal notice and comment rulemaking and informal engagements, we received suggestions on how to update the Certification Program to meet current market needs. This final rule includes deregulatory actions that: take into consideration suggestions and comments received on the Health Data, Technology, and Interoperability: ASTP/ONC Deregulatory Actions To Unleash Prosperity Proposed Rule (90 FR 60970) (“Proposed Rule”); account for the current and future state of technology; reduce burden on health IT developers; and promote innovation for health IT developers, providers, and other interested parties.
These efforts directly align with Administration goals as outlined in E.O. 14192 (Unleashing Prosperity through
( printed page 67917)
Deregulation) [1]
and E.O. 14267 (Reducing Anti-Competitive Regulatory Barriers).[2]
By removing burdensome and unnecessary requirements of the Certification Program, this final rule supports providers in caring for their patients. Developers of certified health IT will have more time to support providers' specific technological needs. Further, by increasing competition in the certified health IT market that will come from reduced barriers to entry for the certification of health IT, providers also will have more choices to meet their health IT needs.
America's interoperability arc in healthcare has bent decisively toward Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources (FHIR®)-based application programming interfaces (APIs). An open, interoperable health data ecosystem invites entrepreneurship, drives innovation, and cements American leadership and competitiveness in the expanding digital health marketplace. As discussed in this deregulatory final rule, we aggressively reduce and remove long-standing functionality-oriented and non-FHIR-based certification criteria from the Certification Program. While this approach will directly and rapidly reduce compliance burdens for health IT developers that participate in the Certification Program, more broadly, it will enable ONC to reset the Certification Program's regulatory scope and establish a new foundation on which to build FHIR-based API requirements in the future. This will allow more creative super intelligence [3]
(SI)-enabled interoperability solutions that combine FHIR with newer standards to emerge, such as Model Context Protocol (MCP), which “standardizes how applications provide context to Large Language Models (LLMs),” [4]
and will further embrace the 21st Century Cures Act (Pub. L. 114-255) (Cures Act)'s reference to successor technology and standards in the API Condition of Certification.[5]
While FHIR provides the potential for better, faster, and more consistent ways to address emerging market needs and policy imperatives, more work is needed for certain use cases. We intend to continue to fully engage industry and our Federal partners, such as CMS, to rapidly advance FHIR specifications for regulatory readiness. We also intend to sharpen the Certification Program's future focus to prioritize FHIR-based APIs that, consistent with all legal requirements: (1) enhance automation and API performance; (2) move beyond read-only interactions; and (3) expand the scope of data available

articles.title: Europe’s central bank chief, Christine Lagarde, steps down for ‘freedom of speech’
articles.summary: Possible candidate to run World Economic Forum departs ECB nine months early, saying she wants to speak her mind about world affairsChristine Lagarde, the eurozone’s top central banker, has said she is stepping down nine months early to speak her mind about world affairs and confront the “misrepresentation of the truth”.Ending months of speculation about her future at the European Central Bank, Lagarde said she would quit her role as president next February rather than October next year because ...
articles.full_text:
Christine Lagarde, the eurozone’s top central banker, has said she is stepping down nine months early to speak her mind about world affairs and confront the “misrepresentation of the truth”.
Ending months of speculation about her future at the European Central Bank, Lagarde said she would quit her role as president next February rather than October next year because the rules of neutrality that governed her job prevented her from influencing debate about financial and economics affairs.
She spoke at the end of a press conference to explain the ECB’s decision to hold interest rates – maintaining its key deposit rate at 2.5% – despite inflation climbing to 3.8% last month, its highest since September 2023.
Lagarde said: “I want to have the freedom of speech, the freedom of expression and the freedom to engage on matters that are not monetary policy matters.”
The former managing director of the International Monetary Fund has been tipped as a candidate to take over the running of the World Economic Forum, which holds its annual meeting in Davos each January. The WEF founder, Klaus Schwab, stepped down last year after being accused of financial and ethical misconduct, which he denies.
Lagarde’s early departure fires the starting gun on the race to replace her as ECB chief, at a time when the eurozone is struggling with weak growth and above-target inflation. Potential candidates include the former Dutch central bank president Klaas Knot, the Spanish banker Pablo Hernández de Cos, the German central bank president, Joachim Nagel, and Nadia Calviño, the president of the European Investment Bank.
The European Council made up of EU heads of state appoints the head of the ECB, which sets monetary policy across the eurozone.
There has been speculation that Lagarde, a former finance minister of France, has been encouraged to quit early by the French president, Emmanuel Macron, so her successor can be appointed before the possibility of a far-right or far-left presidential candidate being elected to the Élysée Palace. Lagarde will also be able to participate in next April’s elections.
She noted that ECB officials were bound by strict rules on not appearing partisan. “We have an obligation of neutrality; we comment on the situation with the focus on monetary policy,” Lagarde said, adding that the mandate was “the price we pay for being independent”.
Lagarde said she no longer felt comfortable staying silent on broader global issues. “I’m interested in the truth, and I see the truth being very often damaged, contradicted by misrepresentation,” she said, without elaborating.
Drawing on more than two decades in international economic and financial roles, she said she had more to contribute. “There are things that I can say – whether people will listen or not is another story. But I feel that I should say those things and I cannot do so in my current position.”
To reassure markets and staff that her early departure would not disrupt the central bank’s operations, she added: “A process has already started to identify my successor.” She said there were “plenty of excellent candidates.”
Macron said on Thursday that the succession at the ECB must be prepared in “an orderly and balanced way” with European partners, and also expressed his deep gratitude to Lagarde for her action during her tenure.
Holger Schmieding, the chief economist at Berenberg bank, said: “The European Union is trying to guard itself at least somewhat against the risk that rightwing Marine Le Pen may win the French presidential election in April/May 2027.
“Lagarde’s successor will still be appointed while the staunchly pro-European centrist Emmanuel Macron still resides in the Élysée Palace. He is a long-term political adversary of Le Pen.”
Lagarde joined the ECB in late 2019, shortly before the start of the Covid pandemic. During her tenure the central bank has also faced the economic consequences of the Russia-Ukraine war, Donald Trump’s trade war and his war in the Middle East.
Lagarde was wearing two plasters on her face in her video message, which she said was because of “a small surgery earlier in the week”. She added: “Follow doctors’ orders and get your skin checked regularly.”

articles.title: DoorDash to buy Instacart for $17bn in major grocery delivery consolidation
articles.summary: Acquisition will supercharge DoorDash’s grocery delivery, ‘one of the hardest things to get right online’, CEO saysDoorDash is gobbling up Instacart in a $17bn acquisition that will supercharge its grocery delivery business.DoorDash said the Instacart brand name and app will remain, and Instacart shoppers can continue fulfilling orders for Instacart. Grocers can also choose to work with Instacart or DoorDash. Instacart customers will now have access to 50,000 additional stores covered by DoorDas...
articles.full_text:
DoorDash is gobbling up Instacart in a $17bn acquisition that will supercharge its grocery delivery business.
DoorDash said the Instacart brand name and app will remain, and Instacart shoppers can continue fulfilling orders for Instacart. Grocers can also choose to work with Instacart or DoorDash. Instacart customers will now have access to 50,000 additional stores covered by DoorDash, the company said.
Instacart, founded in 2012, specializes in grocery and convenience store delivery in the US and Canada. Its 600,000 “shoppers” – who are independent contractors – completed 338m orders last year, according to company filings. Instacart has a market value of $14bn.
DoorDash, founded in San Francisco in 2013, began as a restaurant delivery business but has expanded to pet food and electronics. Operating in 40 countries, it completed more than 3bn orders last year using a network of 9m independent delivery workers. It has a market value of $73bn.
DoorDash began delivering groceries in 2020 amid a surge in pandemic-era demand. Grocers were initially cautious. Kroger partnered with the San Francisco company in 2022 but initially allowed the company to deliver only flowers, sushi and prepared meals from a limited number of stores.
The partnership with one of the nation’s largest grocery chains expanded last fall, and DoorDash now lists the full inventory of all 2,700 US Kroger stores in its online marketplace. DoorDash scored another coup last month when it added delivery from Costco .
Tony Xu, co-founder and CEO of DoorDash, said the acquisition will combine Instacart’s expertise in grocery with DoorDash’s expertise in logistics and delivery.
“Grocery is one of the hardest things to get right online. Someone has to pick a ripe avocado, find a substitute you’d choose yourself, and get the ice cream to you before it melts,” Xu said in a statement. “Together, we could give stores of every size more of those tools and unlock the potential of grocery delivery.”
DoorDash’s aggressive market-share gains have hurt Instacart. Five years ago, Instacart commanded 26% of spending on US delivery platforms; that share has fallen to 18%, according to Consumer Edge, a market research company. DoorDash’s share grew from 44% to 59% in that same period. Uber Eats’ share held steady at just under 20%.
It’s not yet clear what the deal will mean for some partnerships. Instacart offers delivery from Walmart, for example, but DoorDash stopped providing Walmart delivery in 2022.

articles.title: US economy grows faster than expected but inflation rises to 3.7%
articles.summary: Commerce department data contrasts with sharp deterioration in consumer sentiment as midterms loomThe US economy grew faster than expected in the third quarter while inflation accelerated in September, according to new commerce department data released on Thursday, less than a week before the midterm elections that will determine control of Congress.Gross domestic product (GDP) increased at a 3.4% annualized rate last quarter, the commerce department’s ⁠bureau of economic analysis said in its ad...
articles.full_text:
The US economy grew faster than expected in the third quarter while inflation accelerated in September, according to new commerce department data released on Thursday, less than a week before the midterm elections that will determine control of Congress.
Gross domestic product (GDP) increased at a 3.4% annualized rate last quarter, the commerce department’s bureau of economic analysis said in its advance estimate of the third-quarter GDP on Thursday. Economists polled by Reuters had forecast GDP advancing at a 3.2% pace.
Estimates ranged from a 1% growth rate to a 4.2% pace.
The growth comes as resilient consumer spending and AI-driven business investment has more than offset the impact of higher oil prices stemming from the conflict in the Middle East.
The change is in stark contrast to households’ downbeat assessment of the economy, reflected in Donald Trump’s record-low approval ratings and a sharp deterioration in consumer sentiment.
The economy is expanding at a pace that is well above what some Federal Reserve officials regard as the non-inflationary growth rate of about 2%. New data from the personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index, the Fed’s preferred measure of inflation, showed that prices increased 0.5% for the month in September and the annualized inflation rate rose to 3.6%. In August, the PCE’s inflation rate was 3.4%.
Core inflation, which excludes volatile food and energy prices, rose to an annualized 3.1%.
The consumer price index, a separate measure of inflation released by the Department of Labor that was released earlier in October, had also shown inflation rising in September, with the annualized inflation rate going from 3.4% in August to 3.7% in September.
Despite the rise in prices, the US central bank on Wednesday left its benchmark interest rate in the 3.75%-4% range while acknowledging that inflation “remains elevated”.
Increasing interest rates can slow inflation, at the risk of slackening economic activity and the jobs market. Because inflation is still hot, economists expect the Fed to raise rates in December. The Fed chairman, Kevin Warsh, told reporters “economic activity is expanding at a strong pace,” noting that “while uncertainty remains, owing in part to geopolitical developments, domestic spending has been resilient.”
Given the increasing dominance of AI-related spending, some economists said the strong GDP growth was probably not a true picture of the economy. Investors are increasingly focusing on the rising costs of long-term AI projects, in which the payoff is uncertain. Tech firms have borrowed huge sums over the past year for AI spending, a potential downside risk to equipment spending. Still, economists did expect this pillar of support to weaken, though a pullback in spending was likely.
Consumer spending, which accounts for more than two-thirds of the economy, increased at a 3.8% pace in the July-September quarter after growing at a 3.8% rate in the second quarter. Historically low layoffs and moderate hiring are helping to underpin spending, though wage gains have at times lagged behind inflation.
But households also have been saving less and dipping into their nest eggs to fund spending. With average gasoline prices still above $4 a gallon – about $1 a gallon more than a year ago – as the US-Israel war on Iran drags on, economists anticipate a slowdown in consumer spending.
Multiple polls have shown Donald Trump’s approval rating on the economy have plummeted in the weeks before the election, with voters citing frustration over rising gas and grocery prices. Overall consumer sentiment, measured by the University of Michigan is down 15% from February, before the start of the war with Iran, as consumers expect more inflation to come.
