AGENCY:
Office of Child Support Enforcement (OCSE), Administration for Children and Families (ACF), Department of Health and Human Services (HHS or the Department).
ACTION:
Final rule.
SUMMARY:
This final rule amends the Child Support regulations that were unnecessary or obsolete in the following sections: State Plan Approval and Grant Procedures, State Plan Requirements, Standards for Program Operations, Federal Financial Participation, Program Performance Measures, Standards, Financial Incentives, and Penalties, Computerized Support Enforcement Systems, Annual State Self-Assessment Review and Report, Tribal Child Support Enforcement (IV-D) Program, and Computerized Tribal IV-D Systems and Office Automation.
DATES:
This rule is effective on November 30, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Adam N. Jones, Deputy Chief of Staff, Immediate Office of the Assistant Secretary, Administration for Children and Families, Department of Health and Human Services, Washington, DC, 202-417-0115 or
Deregulation@acf.hhs.gov.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Statutory Authority
This rule is published under the authority granted to the Secretary of Health and Human Services by section 1102 of the Social Security Act (the Act), 42 U.S.C. 1302. Section 1102 of the Act authorizes the Secretary to publish regulations, not inconsistent with the Act, which “may be necessary for efficient administration of the functions for which the Secretary is responsible under the Act.” This rule is also published in accordance with section 455(f) of the Act, 42 U.S.C. 655(f). Section 455(f) authorizes the Secretary to issue regulations governing the grants to Tribes and Tribal organizations operating child support programs.
II. Background
The Child Support Enforcement Program, established under Title IV-D of the Social Security Act, is a Federal-State-Tribal partnership designed to help children receive financial support from their noncustodial parents. The program operates through State and Tribal child support agencies that provide child support enforcement services including locating noncustodial parents, establishing paternity, establishing and enforcing support orders, and collecting and distributing child support payments. Since the program's establishment in 1975, OCSE has worked with States and Tribes to improve the effectiveness and efficiency of child support program operations. Over time, Congress has amended Title IV-D to expand and refine program responsibilities, and ACF has promulgated implementing regulations to support consistent national administration of the program while providing flexibility to States and Tribes.
See, e.g.,40 FR 27156 (June 26, 1975) (initial implementation of the Child Support Enforcement Program regulations); 54 FR 15761 (Apr. 19, 1989) (revising interstate and enforcement procedures to improve program effectiveness); 57 FR 30658 (July 10, 1992) (implementing Family Support Act amendments and strengthening automated processing and distribution requirements); 63 FR 44795 (Aug. 21, 1998) (implementing provisions of the Personal Responsibility and Work Opportunity Reconciliation Act of 1996 related to program automation); 69 FR 16638 (Mar. 30, 2004) (implementing direct funding of Tribal Child Support Enforcement programs); and 81 FR 93492 (Dec. 20, 2016) (modernizing child support program operations and emphasizing family-centered enforcement approaches).
ACF has determined many of these regulations were originally adopted during periods of substantial statutory expansion of the Title IV-D program, when ACF sought to provide introductory program descriptions, restate newly enacted statutory requirements, promote national consistency during early implementation efforts, or codify administrative practices that were not yet well established among State agencies.
See, e.g.,40 FR 27156, 27160-61 (describing the need for foundational regulations to establish uniform State plan requirements during initial implementation of Title IV-D); 57 FR 30658, 30659-60 (explaining that several provisions were intended to clarify statutory responsibilities and standardize administration among States); 63 FR 44795, 44795-96 (stating that certain amendments were intended to codify statutory changes enacted by Personal Responsibility and Work Opportunity Reconciliation Act of 1996 (PRWORA) and provide operational guidance to States during implementation); and 81 FR 93492, 93493-95 (describing the purpose of regulatory amendments as improving program flexibility and modernizing existing practices). In several instances, prior preambles explained that the regulations were intended primarily to clarify statutory requirements, provide organizational context, or assist States during transitions following major legislative amendments.
ACF has also determined that many of those rationales no longer support maintaining these provisions in the Code of Federal Regulations (CFR) because the Title IV-D program has matured substantially and State and Tribal agencies now operate within a well-established statutory and administrative framework supported by decades of program guidance, policy issuances, automated systems requirements, and operational practice. In addition, Congress has amended Title IV-D numerous times to codify core program requirements directly in statute, thereby reducing any independent regulatory effect of certain provisions. As a result, ACF has concluded that retaining regulations that restate statutory text, provide historical or descriptive information without imposing substantive obligations, or address matters more appropriately administered through sub-regulatory guidance and technical
( printed page 68046)
assistance, is no longer necessary to ensure effective administration of the Title IV-D program.

Published Document: 2026-22093 (91 FR 68013)
This document has been published in the Federal Register. Use the PDF linked in the document sidebar for the official electronic format.
( printed page 68013)
AGENCY:
Office of Personnel Management.
ACTION:
Final rule.
SUMMARY:
The Office of Personnel Management (OPM) is issuing a final rule to modernize the framework governing personnel management and strategic human capital management in Federal agencies. This rule amends the regulatory framework for personnel management in Federal agencies to streamline human capital planning and reporting requirements, strengthen the authority of agency Chief Human Capital Officers (CHCOs), update employee survey requirements, and align the regulatory framework with Executive branch priorities for a high-performing Federal workforce. OPM carefully considered all public comments received on the proposed rule and has made targeted revisions in response.
DATES:
Effective November 30, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Jeanne Jacobson, Acting Deputy Associate Director, Center for Workforce Strategy, Design, and Insights, Office of Personnel Management, 1900 E Street NW, Washington, DC 20415; email:
workforce@opm.gov;
phone (202) 606-1800.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Background
The Civil Service Reform Act (CSRA) of 1978 established the foundational framework for merit-based personnel management in the Federal Government. Pursuant to the CSRA and subsequent statutory authority, OPM is responsible for promulgating Governmentwide regulations governing Federal human capital management, including the systems and standards by which agencies plan, implement, and evaluate their human capital strategies.
Part 250 of title 5 of the Code of Federal Regulations establishes the regulatory framework for personnel management in Federal agencies. Subpart A sets standards for agency personnel actions and delegation agreements. Subpart B—Strategic Human Capital Management-defines the systems, standards, and metrics agencies must use to manage human capital, currently organized around the Human Capital Framework (HCF) and the Human Capital Operating Plan (HCOP), Human Capital Reviews (HCR), and HRStat quarterly reviews. Subpart C—Employee Surveys—governs the administration and public disclosure of annual Federal employee surveys and establishes a core set of 16 required survey questions.
On July 2, 2026, OPM published a proposed rule (91 FR 40435) to amend 5 CFR part 250 to modernize strategic human capital management across the Federal Government. The proposed rule proposed to: (1) consolidate and streamline human capital planning requirements by replacing the HCOP, HCR, and HRStat framework with Annual Staffing Plans (ASPs) and associated review processes; (2) strengthen CHCO authority and visibility; (3) require each agency to establish a Strategic Hiring Committee to oversee hiring within the agency; (4) revise the employee survey framework under subpart C, including changes to the Governmentwide core question set and survey administration; and (5) remove references to workforce diversity from the regulatory text.
In response to public comments, OPM has made targeted revisions to the proposed rule. Key changes from the proposed rule include: (1) clarifying the terminology distinguishing strategic human capital planning from operational staffing planning and tying Annual Staffing Plan development to the budget formulation cycle under the annual Office of Management and Budget (OMB) Circular A-11, Preparation, Submission, and Execution of the Budget, Part 6 (OMB, Circular No. A-11, Preparation, Submission, and Execution of the Budget (Aug. 29, 2025),
https://www.whitehouse.gov/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/a11.pdf); (2) adding an annual agency-head-certification requirement to ensure CHCO visibility, oversight, and control; and (3) permitting agencies to integrate Quarterly Staffing Plan Performance Reviews into existing performance review processes. Each of these changes is discussed in detail in the comment-response section below.
In response to comments, OPM also clarifies several matters that do not change the regulatory text, including the effect of the removal of nonstatutory references to a “diverse” workforce and the scope of the Strategic Hiring Committee's role; those clarifications are addressed in the same section.
Digest of Public Comments
In response to the proposed rule, OPM received nine comments during the 30-day public comment period ending August 3, 2026. These responses came from a range of sources: individual citizens; nonprofit and professional organizations; and a former Federal employee writing in a private capacity. All nine comments are substantive and have been considered in full. All comments were posted and made available to the public in the docket. A reference to a comment provides the location of the item in the public record (
i.e.,
the four-digit number associated with the location in the docket) at
https://www.regulations.gov/comment/OPM-2026-0368-nnnn.
The comments are summarized below, together with OPM's responses, including where OPM has adopted, partially adopted, or declined commenter suggestions, along with OPM's reasoning. The comments are organized by issue category.
General Comments
Comment 0010 expressed general support for the proposed rule, noting it “will strengthen accountability, improve hiring practices, and enhance morale and recruitment across the federal workforce.” Comment 0010 offered additional recommendations to strengthen protections against political-to-career conversions (“burrowing in”), discussed further below.
Comments 0002 and 0005 expressed broad opposition to the rule. Comment 0002 argued the rule lacks the required cost-benefit analysis and would negatively affect employee retention and hiring quality. Comment 0005 urged
( printed page 68014)
OPM to abandon the rule, citing concerns about administrative burden, potential for politicization of the civil service, and anticipated harm to scientific, diversity, equity, and inclusion-related roles, to include harmful impacts to sexual and gender orientation focused roles.
Comment 0002 argued that the proposed rule “does not seem to be in compliance with various regulatory requirements” because it lacks a cost-benefit analysis. OPM disagrees. The Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs designated this rulemaking a significant regulatory action under section 3(f) of Executive Order 12866, Regulatory Planning and Review, 58 FR 51735 (Oct. 4, 1993), and OPM has assessed its costs and benefits accordingly. Published Document: 2026-22089 (91 FR 68028)
This document has been published in the Federal Register. Use the PDF linked in the document sidebar for the official electronic format.
AGENCY:
U.S. Customs and Border Protection; the Department of Homeland Security.
ACTION:
Final rule.
SUMMARY:
This document amends U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) regulations by adding the Republic of Malta (Malta) to the list of countries whose pleasure vessels may be issued U.S. cruising licenses. The U.S. Department of State has notified CBP that yachts used and employed exclusively as pleasure vessels and belonging to any resident of the United States are allowed to arrive at and depart from Maltese ports, and to cruise in Maltese waters without complying with formal entry and clearance procedures. Therefore, CBP is extending reciprocal cruising privileges to Maltese-flagged pleasure vessels.
DATES:
This amendment is effective October 29, 2026. These reciprocal privileges became applicable for Malta as of June 10, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
W. Richmond Beevers, Chief, Cargo
( printed page 68029)
Security, Carriers and Restricted Merchandise Branch, Regulations and Rulings, Office of Trade, (202) 325-0084,
ccrbranchcomments@cbp.dhs.gov.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Background
Under 46 U.S.C. 60504, the Secretary of Homeland Security (Secretary) may allow foreign-flagged yachts used only for pleasure to arrive at and depart from U.S. ports and cruise in U.S. waters without paying any duties or fees, provided that the President is satisfied that the foreign country allows yachts owned by U.S. residents and used only for pleasure to arrive at and depart from its ports and cruise in its waters without entering, clearing, or paying any duties or fees. The statute also provides the Secretary discretion to require foreign yachts to obtain cruising licenses and to prescribe the form and conditions of those licenses.
See46 U.S.C. 60504; Public Law 109-304, 9(b), 120 Stat. 1485, 1680-81 (2006).
The Secretary has delegated to the Commissioner of CBP the authority to prescribe and approve cruising licenses for foreign countries under section 4.94(b) of title 19 of the Code of Federal Regulations (CFR).
See
DHS Delegation No. 07010.3, Revision 03.2. Accordingly, CBP has promulgated regulations governing cruising privileges for U.S. and foreign pleasure vessels. Section 4.94(a) of title 19 of the CFR provides that U.S.-documented vessels with a recreational endorsement, used exclusively for pleasure, not engaged in any trade, and not violating the customs or navigation laws of the United States, may proceed from port to port in the United States or to foreign ports without clearing, and is not subject to entry upon its arrival in the United States, as long as they have not visited hovering vessels, received merchandise while in the customs waters beyond the territorial sea, or received merchandise while on the high seas. When returning from a foreign port or place, such pleasure vessels are required to report their arrival pursuant to 19 CFR 4.2.
Generally, foreign-flagged yachts entering the United States are required to comply with the laws applicable to foreign vessels arriving at, departing from, and proceeding between ports of the United States.
See
section 433 of the Tariff Act of 1930, as amended (19 U.S.C. 1433). However, CBP may issue cruising licenses to pleasure vessels from certain countries if it is found that yachts of the United States are exempt from formal entry and clearance procedures (
e.g.,
filing manifests, obtaining permits to proceed, and paying entry and clearance fees) in those countries.
See19 CFR 4.94(b).
To obtain a cruising license, the owner of a foreign-flagged yacht must file an application with a port director. 19 CFR 4.94(c). If CBP issues a foreign-flagged yacht a cruising license, the yacht may arrive at and depart from the United States and cruise in specified waters of the United States without entering and clearing, without filing manifests and obtaining or delivering permits to proceed, and without the payment of certain fees.
Id.
Such fees include entrance and clearance fees, fees for receiving manifests and granting permits to proceed, duty on tonnage, tonnage tax, or light money.
Id.
A port director may issue a cruising license for a period not to exceed one year.
Id.
Upon arrival at each port in the United States, the master of a foreign-flagged yacht with a cruising license must report the fact of arrival to the appropriate CBP office.
Id.
Section 4.94(b) sets forth the list of countries whose yachts are eligible for cruising licenses.
By diplomatic note dated February 4, 2026, the Embassy of the Republic of Malta, in Washington, DC, informed the Department of State that Malta allows yachts from the United States, used exclusively as pleasure vessels and belonging to any resident of the United States, to arrive at and depart from Maltese ports, and to cruise in the waters of Malta without entering and clearing Maltese Customs and without the payment of any related charges for entry or clearance, dues, duty per ton, tonnage, taxes, or charges for a cruising license. By letter dated June 10, 2026, the Department of State advised the Chief, Cargo Security, Carriers and Restricted Merchandise Branch, CBP, that the Maltese treatment of U.S. pleasure vessels in Maltese waters appears to satisfy the conditions for reciprocal privileges and therefore recommended that Malta be added to the list of countries under the provisions of 19 CFR 4.94(b).
The Chief, Cargo Security, Carriers and Restricted Merchandise Branch, has determined that satisfactory evidence has been furnished to grant the reciprocal privileges allowed under 19 CFR 4.94(b), effective June 10, 2026. Accordingly, under the authority of 46 U.S.C. 60504, Maltese-flagged yachts used only for pleasure may proceed from port to port in the United States or to foreign ports without clearing and are not subject to entry upon arrival at a U.S. port, including the payment of any duties or fees. This final rule revises the list of countries in 19 CFR 4.94(b) to include Malta for the above reasons.
Administrative Procedure Act
CBP has initiated this rulemaking pursuant to an exchange of diplomatic notes between the U.S. Department of State and the Embassy of the Republic of Malta. This rule implements the reciprocal cruising privileges established through that diplomatic exchang

Published Document: 2026-22078 (91 FR 68043)
This document has been published in the Federal Register. Use the PDF linked in the document sidebar for the official electronic format.
AGENCY:
Coast Guard, Department of Homeland Security.
ACTION:
Final rule.
SUMMARY:
The Coast Guard is establishing a safety zone for certain navigable waters of the Sanders Ferry, near Hendersonville, TN. This safety zone is necessary to protect personnel, vessels, and the marine environment from potential hazards during a fireworks show at various times from October 29, 2026, through October 31, 2026. This rulemaking prohibits entry of vessels or persons into this safety zone during enforcement periods unless specifically authorized by the Captain of the Port, Ohio Valley or their designated representative.
DATES:
This rule is effective from 7:15 a.m. local time on October 29, 2026, through 5:30 p.m. local time on October 31, 2026.
If you have questions about this rule, contact MST3 Zachary T. Epps, Sector Ohio Valley Waterways Management Division, U.S. Coast Guard; telephone (206) 815-7006, or email
STL-SMB-MSDNASHVILLE@USCG.MIL.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Table of Abbreviations
CFR Code of Federal Regulations
COTP Captain of the Port
DHS Department of Homeland Security
FR Federal Register
NPRM Notice of proposed rulemaking
§ Section
U.S.C. United States Code
II. Background and Authority
On July 17, 2026, an organization notified the Coast Guard that it will sponsor two fireworks displays launched from a barge on the Cumberland River near Sanders Ferry Park in Hendersonville, Tennessee. The first fireworks display (including a 15-minute safety buffer before and afterwards) is scheduled to occur on October 29, 2026, from approximately 7:15 a.m. until 8:15 a.m., Central Time. The second fireworks display is scheduled to occur on October 31, 2026, from approximately 4:45 p.m. until 5:30 p.m., Central Time. On October 16, 2026, the Coast Guard published a notice of proposed rulemaking (NPRM) titled Safety Zone; Cumberland River, Hendersonville, TN (91 FR 65698). In that NPRM, we stated why we issued the NPRM and invited comments on our proposed regulatory action related to this fireworks display.
Under the authority in 46 U.S.C. 70034, the COTP has determined that this rule is necessary to protect personnel, vessels, and the marine environment from potential hazards associated with the fireworks. No vessel or person will be permitted to enter the safety zone without obtaining permission from COTP or their designated representative.
Because of the hazards associated with this event, the Coast Guard finds that under 5 U.S.C. 553(d)(3), good cause exists for making this rule effective less than 30 days after publication in the
Federal Register
because it is impracticable and contrary to the public interest. We must establish this safety zone by October 29, 2026, to protect personnel, vessels, and the marine environment.
III. Discussion of Comments and the Rule
During the comment period that ended on October 23, 2026, we received two comments. Two commenters identified inconsistencies in the NPRM concerning the dates and times of the planned fireworks displays and associated safety-zone enforcement periods. Specifically, the commenters noted that the NPRM contained conflicting references to October 30 and October 31 for the second enforcement period, as well as inconsistent morning enforcement periods for October 29. One commenter also requested clarification regarding the difference between the overall effective period and the periods when the safety zone would be actively enforced; the basis for pre- and post-display safety buffers; the applicable local time zone; notice to mariners; and procedures for requesting entry into the safety zone.
In response to these comments, the Coast Guard has revised the
( printed page 68044)
enforcement periods to accurately reflect the scheduled fireworks displays. The safety zone will be enforced from 7:15 a.m. until 8:15 a.m., on October 29, 2026, and from 4:45 p.m. until 5:30 p.m., on October 31, 2026. It is always standard that in Coast Guard safety zone rulemaking documents refer to the local time at the location of the safety zone, in this case that is Central Daylight Time (CDT). These enforcement periods include a 15-minute safety buffer before and after each fireworks display to allow for final safety preparations, fireworks-launch operations, monitoring for falling debris, post-display safety assessment, and cleanup.
The Coast Guard has also corrected the conflicting references to an October 30 enforcement period and clarified that the safety zone will not be continuously enforced between the two specified enforcement periods. In other words, this safety zone will be enforced for one hour on October 29, 2026, from 7:15 a.m. until 8:15 a.m., and 45 minutes on October 31, 2026, from 4:45 p.m. until 5:30 p.m. The Coast Guard will provide notice of enforcement through a Broadcast Notice to Mariners on VHF-FM channel 16. The Broadcast Notice to Mariners will include information regarding the enforcement periods and may include sponsor contact information for event-related coordination, as appropriate. Only the Captain of the Port (COTP), Ohio Valley or the COTP's designated representative may authorize entry into the safety zone.
This rule establishes a safety zone on all navigable waters of the Cumberland River from mile marker 221.7 to mile marker 222 near Sanders Ferry Park in Hendersonville, Tennessee. During the stated enforcement periods, no vessel or person may enter the safety zone without obtaining permission from COTP or the COTP's designated representative.
IV. Regulatory Analyses
We developed this rule after considering numerous statutes and Executive orders related to rulemaking. Below we summarize our analysis based on a number of these statutes and Executive orders.
A. Impact on Small Entities
The Regulatory Flexibility Act of 1980 (RFA), 5 U.S.C. 601-612, as amended, requires Federal agencies to consider the potential impact of regulations on small entities during rulemaking. The term “small entities” comprises small businesses, not-for-profit organizations that are independently owned and operated and are not dominant in their fields, and governmental jurisdictions with populations of less than 50,000. AGENCY:
Rural Housing Service, USDA.
ACTION:
Final rule.
SUMMARY:
The Rural Housing Service (RHS or the Agency), a Rural Development (RD) agency of the United States Department of Agriculture (USDA), is amending the Single Family Housing Guaranteed Loan Program (SFHGLP) regulation to permit the financing of single family homes with income producing Accessory Dwelling Units (ADUs) and clarify the eligibility of properties with features designed to accommodate home-based operations using non-commercial real estate features.
DATES:
This final rule is effective December 28, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Stephanie Freeman, Finance & Loan Analyst, Single Family Housing Guaranteed Loan Division, Rural Development, U.S. Department of Agriculture, STOP 0784, Room 2250, South Agriculture Building, 1400 Independence Avenue SW, Washington, DC 20250-0784. Telephone: (314) 457-6413; or email:
stephanie.freeman@usda.gov.

Statutory Authority
The SFHGLP is authorized by Section 502(h) of the Housing Act of 1949 (42 U.S.C. 1472(h)), as amended, and implemented by 7 CFR part 3555.
( printed page 68026)
Background
RHS offers programs to develop and enhance housing and critical community infrastructure in rural areas. The Agency provides loans, grants, and loan guarantees for single and multi-family housing, childcare centers, emergency service facilities, hospitals, libraries, nursing homes, schools, and housing for agricultural workers, among other essential projects. RHS partners with non-profits, tribal governments, and state/federal agencies to provide technical assistance and supplementary financing to local communities.
Title V of the Housing Act of 1949 authorizes RHS to provide SFH loan guarantees, providing low and moderate income individuals in rural areas an opportunity to own decent, safe, and sanitary dwellings and related facilities.
To boost homeownership, the federal government has introduced new initiatives providing prospective buyers with greater flexibility to finance properties with ADUs. Growing demand for affordable housing and limited land availability in many rural communities have made financing properties with ADUs increasingly important. Homeowners can create ADUs within or attached to the primary dwelling through attic or basement conversions, building over existing structures like garages, or constructing standalone residential units.
Homeownership options remain limited for many Americans. The Agency recognizes ADUs offer multiple benefits, including expanding a community's housing supply by introducing new and innovative housing typologies of smaller scale, providing more affordable options for low- and moderate-income residents. ADUs also provide borrowers with a means to generate additional income. Together, these benefits support the broader goal of increasing affordable housing stock and promoting long-term homeownership stability.
Discussion of Public Comments
RHS published a proposed rule on March 31, 2026 [91 FR 15914] to amend the Single Family Housing Guaranteed Program (SFHGLP) regulation at 7 CFR part 3555. RHS received comments from 28 respondents, including individuals, interested parties, and associations. One comment received was not applicable to the contents of the rule.
The following summary presents the relevant comments:
Public Comment:
Nineteen respondents supported the proposed rule, stating it would accommodate more buyers in rural America.
Agency's Response:
RHS appreciates the support and has determined no action is required.
Public Comment:
Four respondents expressed support for the proposed rule but recommended expanding eligibility to include small home-based operations with commercial real estate features, as well as clarifying ADU eligibility and income.
Agency's Response:
RHS appreciates the comments. While the rule amends 7 CFR 3555.102(c) to permit properties with home-based businesses, 7 CFR 3555.102(b) will continue to prohibit purchasing or improving property principally used for income-producing purposes to ensure financed properties remain primarily residential. Regarding income, 7 CFR 3555.152(a)(3) states lenders may not use income to calculate an applicant's ratios if they cannot verify the source, if the income is not stable, or if it is unlikely to continue. The Agency determined potential income from an ADU falls into this category and will not include it in income calculations.
Public Comment:
One respondent agreed the proposal would expand housing opportunities in rural America but raised concerns about consistent enforcement, broader policy implications, and RHS' statutory authority.
Agency's Response:
RHS appreciates the comments. The changes fall within the statutory authority granted by the Housing Act of 1949 (42 U.S.C. 1471et seq.), as amended. RHS recognizes ADUs can increase housing supply, offer additional affordable housing options, and support low- and moderate-income households through the receipt of potential supplemental income. These benefits support RHS' rationale for expanding affordable housing opportunities and promoting long-term homeownership stability.
Public Comment:
One respondent expressed support for the proposal and recommended addressing ADU income and room rent income in the final rule.
Agency's Response:
RHS appreciates the comments and recognizes rental income from an ADU can support homeowner financial stability. However, 7 CFR 3555.152(a)(3) states lenders may not use income to calculate an applicant's ratios if they cannot verify the source, if the income is not stable, or if it is unlikely to continue. The Agency determined potential income from an ADU falls into this category and will not include it in income calculations.
Public Comment:
Two respondents expressed support and offered additional suggestions regarding homebuyer education, home-based operations, renovation funding at purchase, expanding the ADU definition to include non-income producing ADUs, and establishing more precise property standards.
Agency's Response:
RHS appreciates these comments and agrees supporting home-based operations is important. As clarified through this rule, properties accommodating a home-based operation are eligible. articles.title: Government corruption a top issue for US midterm voters, exclusive poll finds
articles.summary: Harris poll for Guardian finds 76% believe officials care more about self-enrichment than helping everyday AmericansGovernment corruption has emerged as a top issue in the upcoming US midterm elections, with an overwhelming majority of Americans saying US government officials use their public office for personal financial gain, according to an exclusive Harris poll for the Guardian.Nearly nine out of 10 Americans said that government corruption, as defined as elected officials putting their own ...
articles.full_text:
Government corruption has emerged as a top issue in the upcoming US midterm elections, with an overwhelming majority of Americans saying US government officials use their public office for personal financial gain, according to an exclusive Harris poll for the Guardian.
Nearly nine out of 10 Americans said that government corruption, as defined as elected officials putting their own or their donors’ financial interests ahead of the public’s, is a problem, according to the survey.
Three-quarters (76%) of voters said that elected officials care more about enriching themselves than improving the economy for ordinary people. Voters were more likely to say that government corruption (65%) is more concerning than corporate power (29%). Just under 10% said that neither concerns them.
The rising cost of living is still expected to drive the election, with 36% of voters saying it is the single most important issue to how they plan to vote in the midterms. But in a slate of other issues including immigration, housing costs, abortion, crime and safety and AI, corruption was the next top issue.
The results come after nearly two years of Donald Trump’s second term, where the president has both figuratively and literally reshaped Washington.
The president demolished the historic East Wing of the White House to make way for a $400m ballroom – $335m of which he said is coming from private donors, including companies such as Apple and Nvidia. The federal government is down more than 420,000 workers after Elon Musk was given the power to introduce huge jobs cuts after donating nearly $300m to Trump’s 2024 presidential campaign. Meanwhile, Trump’s sons are running the family’s lucrative cryptocurrency business that has made Trump $1bn since returning to the White House. And Trump himself accepted a $400m private jet as a gift from the Qatari royal family.
These actions have not gone unnoticed. Voters in the Harris poll were twice as likely to say that Republicans have a bigger corruption problem than Democrats. Forty per cent of voters, including 29% of Republicans, said the GOP has a bigger corruption problem. A third (32%) of voters said that both parties have the problem equally, while 21% said that Democrats have the bigger problem.
Independents, whose votes will be key in swing races across the country, were much more likely to say that Republicans have more of a corruption problem, with 34% saying that Republicans have the bigger issue and 13% pointing to Democrats. Most Independents (42%) said that both parties share the problem equally.
The economy as experienced by everyday Americans has been vastly different from the portrait painted by Wall Street. The stock market has been soaring on the back of never-ending AI spending. In early October, both the S&P 500 and tech-heavy Nasdaq stock indices hit record highs.
The gains have been a boon for a relatively small group of Americans. Americans in the top 1% of wealth own half of the stock market while the bottom 50% own just over 1% of the market.
Armed with more funds than ever, America’s wealthiest people have been driving even more donations into elections. After the supreme court’s 2010 Citizens United case removed limits on campaign contributions, each election year has brought in new records of cash. The midterms have already cost $11.2bn in ads, according to NBC News, the most ever for a midterm cycle.
A chunk of these donations are coming from the ultra-rich. Just 40 donors have already contributed $2.5bn to races this year, according to the Brennan Center for Justice. Last week, billionaire Michael Bloomberg announced he was contributing $80m in last-minute funding for Democratic candidates, while Donald Trump said his political action committee was contributing a total of $400m to Republicans.
For everyday Americans, this flood of cash has changed the motivations of elected officials, who many believe will ultimately prioritize themselves and their donors over their constituents. A majority of voters (78%) in the Harris poll agreed that “elected officials care more about enriching themselves than helping people like me”.
“Government corruption has shot up to become the second most important issue in the midterms after cost of living. Americans are triggered by leaders they now see as both responsible for and profiting off their growing economic hardship,” said John Gerzema, CEO of Harris Poll.
Regardless of who ends up controlling Congress after the midterms, voters across the political spectrum are expecting solutions to address the ongoing affordability crisis that is affecting their lives.
Out of a slate of policies to address the cost of living, a third (32%) of voters said that there should be limits on the influence of companies and lobbyists on government decisions. The second most popular policy was removing tariffs (29%), followed by limiting how much companies raise prices on goods (24%).
On Tuesday, voters in California will decide on a ballot measure that could place a one-time 5% wealth tax on billionaires in the state. Tech billionaires have been spending an estimated $1m a day, altogether more than $340m, to fight the measure. Half (50%) of voters in the new poll, including 56% of independents, said that billionaires do not pay their fair share of taxes. Just 28% of Republicans said the same.
Some in corporate America are catching on to the discontent. Last week, the United Airlines CEO, Scott Kirby, said in an interview that he supports a national wealth tax, a comment that got him backlash from some Republicans.
“We should have a national wealth tax – it won’t work by state because people will just move,” he said. “And I think we should have inheritance taxes that get close to 100% at some level. I would pay them.”
This survey was conducted online within the US by The Harris Poll from 22 October to 24 October 2026 among a nationally representative sample of 2,065 US adults, among whom 1,481 are likely to vote in the 2026 midterm elections.

Notice is hereby given that the Delaware River Basin Commission will hold a public hearing on Wednesday,
( printed page 68499)
November 4, 2026. A business meeting will be held the following month on Thursday, December 3, 2026. Both the hearing and the business meeting are open to the public. The public hearing and the business meeting will be conducted virtually.
Public Hearing.
The Commission will conduct the public hearing virtually on November 4, 2026, commencing at 1:30 p.m. Hearing items will include draft dockets for withdrawals, discharges, and other projects that could have a substantial effect on the basin's water resources. A list of the projects scheduled for hearing, including project descriptions, along with links to draft docket decisions and draft resolutions will be posted on the Commission's website,
www.drbc.gov,
in a long form of this notice at least ten days before the hearing date.
Written comments on matters scheduled for hearing on November 4, 2026 will be accepted through 5:00 p.m. on Monday, November 9, 2026.
The public is advised to check the Commission's website periodically during the ten days prior to the hearing date, as items scheduled for hearing may be postponed if additional time is needed to complete the Commission's review. Items also may be added up to ten days prior to the hearing date. In reviewing docket descriptions, the public is asked to be aware that the details of projects may change during the Commission's review, which is ongoing.
Business Meeting.
The business meeting on December 3, 2026 will begin at 10:00 a.m. and will include: adoption of the Minutes of the Commission's September 2, 2026 business meeting; announcements of upcoming meetings and events; a report on hydrologic conditions; reports by the Executive Director and the Commission's General Counsel; and consideration of any items for which a hearing has been completed or is not required. The agenda is expected to include consideration of the resolutions and draft dockets for withdrawals, discharges, and other projects that are subjects of the public hearing on November 4, 2026.
After all scheduled business has been completed and as time allows, the business meeting will be followed by up to one hour of Open Public Comment, an opportunity to address the Commission off the record on any topic concerning management of the Basin's water resources outside the context of a duly noticed, on-the-record public hearing.
There will be no opportunity for additional public comment for the record at the December 3, 2026 business meeting on items for which a hearing was completed on November 4, 2026 or a previous date. Commission consideration on November 4, 2026 of items for which the public hearing is closed may result in approval of the item as proposed, approval with changes, denial, or deferral. When the Commissioners defer an action, they may announce an additional period for written comment on the item, with or without an additional hearing date, or they may take additional time to consider the input they have already received without requesting further public input. Any deferred items will be considered for action at a public meeting of the Commission on a future date.
Advance Registration and Sign-Up for Oral Comment.
Links for registration to attend the virtual public hearing and the business meeting will be posted at
www.drbc.gov
at least ten days before each meeting date. Registrants who wish to comment on the record during the public hearing on November 4, 2026 or to address the Commissioners informally during the Open Public Comment session following the meeting on December 3, 2026 as time allows, will be asked to so indicate when registering. The Commission's public hearing, business meeting, and Open Public Comment session will also be livestreamed on YouTube at
https://www.youtube.com/@DRBC_1961.
For assistance, please contact Ms. Kate Schmidt of the Commission staff, at
kate.schmidt@drbc.gov.
Addresses for Written Comment.
Written comment on items scheduled for hearing may be submitted through the Commission's web-based comment system, a link to which is provided at
www.drbc.gov.
Use of the web-based system ensures that all submissions are captured in a single location and their receipt is acknowledged. Exceptions to the use of this system are available based on need, by submitting your comment and written request to the attention of the Commission Secretary, DRBC, P.O. Box 7360, 25 Cosey Road, West Trenton, NJ 08628-0360. For assistance, please contact Kate Schmidt at
kate.schmidt@drbc.gov.
Accommodation for Special Needs.
Closed captioning will be available on both webinar and live-stream platforms. Those with limited internet access may listen and speak at virtual public meetings of the DRBC using any of several toll-free phone numbers that will be provided to all virtual meeting registrants.
Other individuals in need of an accommodation as provided for in the Americans with Disabilities Act who wish to attend the virtual hearing or business meeting should contact the Commission Secretary directly at 609-477-7203 or through the Telecommunications Relay Services (TRS) at 711, to discuss how we can accommodate your needs.
Additional Information, Contacts.
Additional public records relating to hearing items may be examined at the Commission's offices by appointment by contacting Donna Woolf, 609-477-7222. For other questions concerning hearing items, please contact David Kovach, Project Review Manager, at 609-477-7264.
Authority.
Delaware River Basin Compact, Public Law 87-328, Approved December 27, 1961, 75 Statutes at Large, 688, sec. 14.4.
Dated: October 22, 2026.
Naomi Mendelsohn,
Commission Secretary and Assistant General Counsel.

On the basis of the record [1]
developed in the subject five-year review, the United States International Trade Commission (“Commission”) determines, pursuant to the Tariff Act of 1930 (“the Act”), that revocation of the antidumping duty order on diamond sawblades and parts thereof from China would be likely to lead to continuation or recurrence of material injury to an industry in the United States within a reasonably foreseeable time.[2]
Background
The Commission instituted this review on March 2, 2026 (91 FR 10131) and determined on June 5, 2026 that it would conduct an expedited review (91 FR 41084, July 6, 2026).
The Commission made this determination pursuant to section 751(c) of the Act (19 U.S.C. 1675(c)). It completed and filed its determination in this review on October 28, 2026. The views of the Commission are contained in USITC Publication 5807 (October 2026), entitled
Diamond Sawblades and Parts Thereof from China: Investigation No. 731-TA-1092 (Third Review).
By order of the Commission.
Issued: October 28, 2026.
Lisa Barton,
Secretary to the Commission.

ACTION:
Notice of meeting.
Pursuant to United States Code, Title 31, section 5135(b)(8)(C), the United States Mint announces a Citizens Coinage Advisory Committee (CCAC) public meeting.
                    Date:
                     November 17, 2026.
                
                    Time:
                     9:00 a.m. to 3:30 p.m. (ET).
                
                    Location:
                     United States Mint, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania.
                
                    Subject:
                     Approval of the Fiscal Year 2026 CCAC Annual Report, and review and discussion of the reverse design portfolios for the 2028 American Youth Sports quarters and Paralympic half dollar.
                
                    Due to the secure nature of the meeting location, members of the public 
                    will not
                     be admitted. Interested members of the public may watch the meeting via live stream on the United States Mint's YouTube Channel at 
                    https://www.youtube.com/user/usmint.
                     To watch the meeting live, members of the public should select the link for the day's CCAC meeting under the “Live” tab.
                
                    The public should call the CCAC HOTLINE at (202) 354-7502 for the latest updates on meeting time and access information.

The CCAC advises the Secretary of the Treasury on any theme or design proposals relating to circulating coinage, bullion coinage, Congressional Gold Medals, and national and other medals; advises the Secretary of the Treasury with regard to the events, persons, or places to be commemorated by the issuance of commemorative coins in each of the five calendar years succeeding the year in which a commemorative coin designation is made; and makes recommendations with respect to the mintage level for any commemorative coin recommended.

articles.title: Notice of Meeting of the National Parks Overflights Advisory Group
articles.summary: The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) and the National Park Service (NPS), in accordance with the National Parks Air Tour Management Act of 2000 (NPATMA), announce the next meeting of the National Parks Overflights Advisory Group (NPOAG). This notification provides the date, location, and agenda for the meeting.
articles.full_text:
AGENCY:
Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), Department of Transportation (DOT).
                    ACTION:
Notice of meeting.
                    SUMMARY:
The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) and the National Park Service (NPS), in accordance with the National Parks Air Tour Management Act of 2000 (NPATMA), announce the next meeting of the National Parks Overflights Advisory Group (NPOAG). This notification provides the date, location, and agenda for the meeting.
                    DATES:
The NPOAG will meet on November 3, 2026, from 10:00 a.m. ET-3:30 p.m. ET.
                    ADDRESSES:
The meeting will take place at the Department of Transportation Volpe Center, 220 Binney St., Cambridge, MA 02142. This NPOAG meeting is open to the public.
            
                SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Background
NPATMA, enacted on April 5, 2000, as Public Law 106-181, required the establishment of the NPOAG within one year after its enactment. NPATMA requires that the NPOAG be a balanced group of representatives of general aviation, commercial air tour operations, environmental concerns, and Native American tribes. The Administrator of the FAA and the Director of NPS (or their designees) serve as ex officio members of the group. Representatives of the Administrator and Director serve alternating 1-year terms as chairperson of the advisory group.
The duties of the NPOAG include providing advice, information, and recommendations to the FAA Administrator and the NPS Director on implementation of Public Law 106-181; quiet aircraft technology; other measures that might accommodate interests to visitors of national parks; and at the request of the Administrator and the Director, on safety, environmental, and other issues related to commercial air tour operations over national parks or tribal lands.
II. Agenda for November 3, 2026, NPOAG Meeting
The agenda for the meeting will include, but is not limited to, air tour reporting, competitive bidding, and quiet technology.
III. Attendance at the Meeting and Submission of Written Comments
                    Although this is not a public meeting, interested persons may attend. Because seating is limited, please contact the person listed under 
                    FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT
                     no later than Nov 2, 2026, if you plan to attend so that meeting space may be made to accommodate all attendees. Written comments regarding the meeting will be accepted directly from attendees or may be sent to the person listed under 
                    FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT
                    .
                
IV. Record of the Meeting
                    If you cannot attend the NPOAG meeting, a summary of the meeting will be made available by contacting the person listed under 
                    FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT
                    .
                
                    Issued in Washington, DC, on October 28, 2026.
Eric Elmore,
Senior Policy Advisor, Federal Aviation Administration—Office of Environment and Energy.

ACTION:

SUMMARY:
The Department of the Treasury, as part of its continuing effort to reduce paperwork and respondent burden, invites the general public and other Federal agencies to take this opportunity to comment on proposed and/or continuing information collections, as required by the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995. Currently, the Community Development Financial Institutions Fund (CDFI Fund), Department of the Treasury, is soliciting comments concerning the New Markets Tax Credit Program (NMTC Program) Community Development Entity (CDE) Certification Application, which Applicants will submit through the CDFI Fund's Awards Management Information System (AMIS).
DATES:
Written comments must be received on or before December 29, 2026 to be assured of consideration.
ADDRESSES:
You may submit comments via the Federal eRulemaking Portal at
www.regulations.gov
Docket No. CDFI-2026-0201. Follow the instructions on the website for the submission of comments. In general, all comments will be available for inspection at
www.regulations.gov.
Comments, including attachments and other supporting materials, are part of the public record. Do not submit any information in your comments or supporting materials that you consider confidential or inappropriate for public disclosure.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Requests for additional information should be directed to Shannon McKay, Acting Program Manager for the Office of Certification Policy and Evaluation, CDFI Fund, U.S. Department of the Treasury, 1500 Pennsylvania Ave. NW, Washington, DC 20220 or by phone at (202) 653-0300. Other information regarding the CDFI Fund and its programs may be obtained through the CDFI Fund's website at
http://www.cdfifund.gov.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
( printed page 68601)
Title:
New Markets Tax Credit Program Community Development Entity (CDE) Certification Application.
OMB Control Number:
1559-0014.
Abstract:
Title I, subtitle C, section 121 of the Community Renewal Tax Relief Act of 2000 (the Act), as enacted in the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2001 (Pub. L. 106-554, December 21, 2000), amended the Internal Revenue Code (IRC) by adding IRC 45D and created the NMTC Program. The Department of the Treasury, through the CDFI Fund, administers the NMTC Program, which provides an incentive to investors in the form of tax credits over seven years, expected to stimulate the provision of private investment capital that, in turn, will facilitate economic and community development in low-income communities. In order to qualify for an allocation of tax credits through the NMTC Program, an entity must be certified as a qualified CDE and submit an allocation application to the CDFI Fund. Nonprofit entities and for-profit entities may be certified as CDEs by the CDFI Fund. In order to be certified as a CDE, an entity must be a domestic corporation or partnership, that: (1) has a primary mission of serving or providing investment capital for low-income communities or low-income persons; and (2) maintains accountability to residents of low-income communities through their representation on any governing or advisory board of the entity.
The CDE Certification Application is being updated to ensure that Applicants are meeting the statutory and regulatory disclosure requirements as well as protecting government resources in alignment with Administration priorities where appropriate. The specific changes include: (1) removal of references to “Minority-Owned or Controlled” in terms of Applicant's structure; (2) addition of a new subsection on “Affiliate Information” to gather information about ownership, control, and foreign interests for affiliates; (3) addition of a new subsection on “Government Investigations and Enforcement” to gather more information on government investigations, enforcement actions and related matters; and (4) additional detailed language for federal anti-discrimination, alignment with specific Executive Orders, and prevention of fraud, waste, and abuse.
Current Actions:
Revision of currently approved collection.
Type of Review:
Regular.
Form:
CDE Certification Application.
Affected Public:
CDEs and entities seeking CDE certification, including business or other for-profit institutions, nonprofit entities, and State, local and Tribal entities.
Estimated Number of Respondents:
150.

Annually.
Estimated Total Number of Annual Responses:
150.
Estimated Annual Time per Respondent:
4 hours.

600 hours.
Request for Comments:
Comments submitted in response to this notice will be summarized and/or included in the request for OMB approval. All comments will become a matter of public record at
http://www.cdfifund.gov.
The CDFI Fund is seeking input on the content of the revised CDE Certification Application. The application and related guidance may be obtained on the CDFI Fund's website at
https://www.cdfifund.gov/programs-training/certification/cde.
Comments are invited on: (a) Whether the collection of information is necessary for the proper performance of the functions of the CDFI Fund, including whether the information shall have practical utility; (b) the accuracy of the CDFI Fund's estimate of the burden of the collection of information; (c) ways to enhance the quality, utility, and clarity of the information to be collected; (d) ways to minimize the burden of the collection of information on respondents, including through the use of technology; and (e) the accuracy of the estimates of the burden of the information collections.

The Cleveland Cuyahoga County Port Authority, grantee of FTZ 40, submitted
( printed page 68490)
a notification of proposed production activity to the FTZ Board (the Board) on behalf of Atlantic Veal & Lamb, LLC for the company's facilities in Creston and Sterling, Ohio, within Subzone 40Q. The notification conforming to the requirements of the Board's regulations (15 CFR 400.22) was received on September 30, 2026.
Pursuant to 15 CFR 400.14(b), FTZ production activity would be limited to the specific foreign-status material(s)/component(s) and specific finished product(s) described in the submitted notification (summarized below) and subsequently authorized by the Board. The benefits that may stem from conducting production activity under FTZ procedures are explained in the background section of the Board's website—accessible via
www.trade.gov/ftz.
The proposed finished products include: bovine products (chilled carcasses, half carcasses, and sectioned carcasses; chilled bone-in primal and subprimals; chilled boneless primal and subprimal cuts; cured, dried, or smoked meat; cured, dried, or smoked offal; tallow; fat; frozen carcasses, half carcasses, and sectioned carcasses; frozen bone-in primal and subprimals; frozen boneless primal and subprimal cuts; edible bones; frozen edible offal; frozen tongues; boneless, chilled veal trim and manufacturing beef; boneless, frozen veal trim and manufacturing beef; raw breaded or battered cutlets, chops, and portioned cuts; raw breaded or battered bone-in chops and racks; raw seasoned or marinated cuts, cutlets, and chops; raw seasoned or formulated ground patties; raw, ready to cook, formulated meatloaf and meatballs; cooked prepared dishes, including braised shanks, with or without sauce; ready to eat cured, smoked, and fully cooked; unformulated concentrated extract; bone broth, stock, and concentrated stock); sheep products (tallow; fat; edible bones; fresh lamb carcasses and half carcasses; fresh bone in lamb; fresh boneless lamb; frozen lamb carcasses and half carcasses; frozen bone in lamb; frozen boneless lamb; seasoned, breaded, or cooked; seasoned, breaded, or cooked lamb; bone broth, stock, and concentrated stock); raw, ready to cook, formulated bovine and pork meat; and, demi-glace, fond, sauce base, and soup base containing meat extract (duty rate ranges from duty-free to 6.
4% and from 0.
43¢/kg to 4.
4¢/kg).

The proposed foreign-status materials/components include: bovine components (chilled carcasses, half carcasses, and sectioned carcasses; chilled bone-in primal and subprimals; chilled boneless primal and subprimal cuts; cured, dried, or smoked meat; cured, dried, or smoked offal; tallow; fat; frozen carcasses, half carcasses, and sectioned carcasses; frozen bone-in primal and subprimals; frozen boneless primal and subprimal cuts; edible bones; frozen edible offal; frozen tongues; boneless, chilled veal trim and manufacturing beef; boneless, frozen veal trim and manufacturing beef); and sheep components (tallow; fat; edible bones; fresh lamb carcasses and half carcasses; fresh lamb bone in; fresh lamb boneless; frozen lamb carcasses and half carcasses; frozen lamb bone in, frozen lamb boneless) (duty rate ranges from duty-free to 2.3% and from 0.43¢/kg to 4.4¢/kg).
The request indicates that certain materials/components are subject to duties under section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, depending on the country of origin. The applicable section 301 decisions require subject merchandise to be admitted to FTZs in privileged foreign status (19 CFR 146.41).

ftz@trade.gov.

A copy of the notification will be available for public inspection in the “Online FTZ Information System” section of the Board's website.

Published Document: 2026-22233 (91 FR 68492)
This document has been published in the Federal Register. Use the PDF linked in the document sidebar for the official electronic format.
AGENCY:
Enforcement and Compliance, International Trade Administration, Department of Commerce.
SUMMARY:
The U.S. Department of Commerce (Commerce) determines that Société Nouvelle des Couleurs Zinciques (SNCZ) did not make sales of strontium chromate from France in the United States at less than normal value (NV) during the period of review (POR) November 1, 2023, through October 31, 2024.
DATES:
Applicable October 30, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Jonathan Schueler or Rachel Accorsi, AD/CVD Operations, Office VIII, Enforcement and Compliance, International Trade Administration, U.S. Department of Commerce, 1401 Constitution Avenue NW, Washington, DC 20230; telephone: (202) 482-9175 or (202) 482-3149, respectively.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Background
On May 8, 2026, Commerce published the
Preliminary Results
of this administrative review in the
Federal Register
.[1]
Between June 1 and 5, 2026, Commerce conducted verification of SNCZ in Beauchamp, France.[2]
On August 7, 2026, Commerce extended the deadline for the final results until October 28, 2026.[3]
On August 21, 2026, Commerce invited interested parties to comment on the
Preliminary Results
and SNCZ's Verification Report.[4]
No interested party submitted a case brief. Commerce conducted this review in accordance with section 751(a)(1)(B) of the Tariff Act of 1930, as amended (the Act).
The product covered by this
Order
is strontium chromate from France. For a complete description of the scope of the
Order, see
the
Preliminary Results
PDM.
Verification
As provided in section 782(i) of the Act, in June 2026, Commerce conducted on-site verification of the sales and cost data reported by SNCZ. We used standard verification procedures, including an examination of relevant accounting and sales records, and original source documentation provided by SNCZ.[6]
Changes Since the Preliminary Results
Commerce is implementing certain changes due to verification findings that have no impact on the dumping margin.[7]
As no parties submitted comments regarding the
Preliminary Results
or Commerce's verification findings, we made no further changes to the
Preliminary Results
and no decision memorandum accompanies this notice.
Final Results of Review
As a result of this review, we determine the following weighted-average dumping margin exists for the POR, November 1, 2023, through October 31, 2024:
Exporter or producer
Weighted-average dumping margin
(percent)
Société Nouvelle des Couleurs Zinciques
0.00
Disclosure
Commerce intends to disclose to parties in this proceeding the calculations performed for these final results of review within five days of a public announcement or, if there is no public announcement, within five days of the date of publication of the notice of final results in the
Federal Register
, in accordance with 19 CFR 351.224(b).
Assessment Rates
Pursuant to section 751(a)(2)(C) of the Act, and 19 CFR 351.212(b)(1), Commerce has determined, and U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) shall assess, antidumping duties on all appropriate entries of subject merchandise in accordance with the final results of this review. As there are no entered values on the record for SNCZ's sales, pursuant to 19 CFR 351.212(b)(1), we calculated importer-specific per-unit duty assessment rates based on the ratio of the total amount of dumping calculated for the examined sales to the total quantity of those sales. To determine whether an importer-specific per-unit duty assessment rate is
de minimis,
we calculated an estimated entered value. If either SNCZ's weighted-average dumping margin is zero or
de minimis
within the meaning of 19 CFR 351.106(c), or an importer-specific assessment rate is zero or
de minimis,
we instruct CBP to liquidate the appropriate entries without regard to antidumping duties.[8]
Accordingly, because SNCZ's weighted-average dumping margin is zero percent, we will instruct CBP to liquidate the appropriate entries without regard to antidumping duties.
Commerce's “reseller policy” will apply to entries of subject merchandise during the POR produced by the company included in these final results of review for which the reviewed company did not know that the merchandise it sold to the intermediary (
e.g.,
a reseller, trading company, or exporter) was destined for the United States. In such instance, we will instruct CBP to liquidate unreviewed entries at the all-others rate if there is no rate for
( printed page 68493)
the intermediate company(ies) involved in the transaction.[9]
Commerce intends to issue assessment instructions to CBP no earlier than 35 days after the date of publication of the final results of this review in the
Federal Register
. If a timely summons is filed at the U.S. Court of International Trade, the assessment instructions will direct CBP not to liquidate relevant entries until the time for parties to file a request for a statutory injunction has expired (
i.e.,
within 90 days of publication).
Cash Deposit Requirements
The following deposit requirements will be effective for all shipments of the subject merchandise entered, or withdrawn from warehouse, for consumption on or after the publication date of the final results of this administrative review, as provided by section 751(a)(2)(C) of the Act: (1) the cash deposit rate for SNCZ will be equal to the weighted-average dumping margin established in the final results of this administrative review (
i.e.,
0.00 percent); (2) for merchandise exported by a producer or exporter not covered in this review but covered in a prior segment of the proceeding, the cash deposit rate will continue to be the company-specific rate published for the most recently completed segment of this proceeding in which the producer or exporter participated; (3) if the exporter is not a firm covered in this review, a prior review, or the original less-than-fair-value (LTFV) investigation, but the producer is, the cash deposit rate will be the rate established for the most recently completed segment of the proceeding for the producer of the merchandise; and (4) the cash deposit rate for all other producers and exporters will continue to be 32.16 percent
ad valorem,
the all-others rate established in the LTFV investigation.[10]
These cash deposit requirements, when imposed, shall remain in effect until further notice.
Notification to Importers Regarding the Reimbursement of Duties
This notice serves as a final reminder to importers of their responsibility under 19 CFR 351.402(f)(2) to file a certificate regarding the reimbursement of antidumping duties prior to liquidation of the relevant entries during the POR. Failure to comply with this requirement could result in Commerce's presumption that reimbursement of antidumping duties occurred and the subsequent assessment of double antidumping duties.

articles.title: Foreign-Trade Zone (FTZ) 38, Notification of Proposed Production Activity; ElringKlinger South Carolina, LLC; (Automotive Battery Subassemblies); Easley, South Carolina
articles.full_text:
ElringKlinger South Carolina, LLC submitted a notification of proposed production activity to the FTZ Board (the Board) for its facility in Easley, South Carolina within FTZ 38. The notification conforming to the requirements of the Board's regulations (15 CFR 400.22) was received on September 24, 2026.
                    Pursuant to 15 CFR 400.14(b), FTZ production activity would be limited to the specific foreign-status material(s)/component(s) and specific finished product(s) described in the submitted notification (summarized below) and subsequently authorized by the Board. The benefits that may stem from conducting production activity under FTZ procedures are explained in the background section of the Board's website—accessible via 
                    www.trade.gov/ftz.
The proposed finished products include: battery cell interconnection assembly; battery distribution and sensing assembly; and flexible printed circuit (duty rate ranges from duty-free to 3.4%).
The proposed foreign-status materials/components include: cleaning paste; plastic resin; insulating plastic film; plastic protective cover; steel bolts; steel screws; copper busbar; aluminum sheet; aluminum connector; plastic support used to secure busbar; plastic fastener for screws; flexible printed circuit; flexible electrical connector; and plastic carrier used to support busbar (duty rate ranges from duty-free to 8.5%).
The request indicates that certain materials/components are subject to duties under section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962 or section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, depending on the country of origin. The applicable section 232 and section 301 decisions require subject merchandise to be admitted to FTZs in privileged foreign status (19 CFR 146.41).
                    Public comment is invited from interested parties. Submissions shall be addressed to the Board's Executive Secretary and sent to: 
                    ftz@trade.gov.
                     The closing period for their receipt is December 9, 2026.
                
A copy of the notification will be available for public inspection in the “Online FTZ Information System” section of the Board's website.
                    For further information, contact John Frye at 
                    John.Frye@trade.gov.
                    Dated: October 27, 2026.
Colin Agostisi,
Executive Secretary.

articles.title: Foreign-Trade Zone (FTZ) 31, Notification of Proposed Production Activity; World Wide Technology; (Networking Racks); Edwardsville, Illinois
articles.full_text:
The America's Central Port District, grantee of FTZ 31, submitted a notification of proposed production activity to the FTZ Board (the Board) on behalf of World Wide Technology (WWT) for WWT's facilities in Edwardsville, Illinois within FTZ 31. The notification conforming to the requirements of the Board's regulations (15 CFR 400.22) was received on October 5, 2026.
                    Pursuant to 15 CFR 400.14(b), FTZ production activity would be limited to the specific foreign-status material(s)/component(s) and specific finished product(s) described in the submitted notification (summarized below) and subsequently authorized by the Board. The benefits that may stem from conducting production activity under FTZ procedures are explained in the background section of the Board's website—accessible via 
                    www.trade.gov/ftz.
The proposed finished product is networking racks (duty free).
The proposed foreign-status materials/components include: hi-speed data networking switches, ethernet networking switches; network management appliances, direct-attach copper cable assemblies; and, optical transceiver modules (duty free).
The request indicates that certain materials/components are subject to duties under section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962 or section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, depending on the country of origin. The applicable section 232 and section 301 decisions require subject merchandise to be admitted to FTZs in privileged foreign status (19 CFR 146.41).
                    Public comment is invited from interested parties. Submissions shall be addressed to the Board's Executive Secretary and sent to: 
                    ftz@trade.gov.
                     The closing period for their receipt is December 9, 2026.
                
A copy of the notification will be available for public inspection in the “Online FTZ Information System” section of the Board's website.

In compliance with the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995 (PRA), this notice announces that the Information Collection Request (ICR) summarized below will be submitted to the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) for review and approval. The ICR describes the nature of the information collection and its expected burden. This document describes a collection of information for which NHTSA intends to seek OMB approval on the State Data Transfer (SDT) program for Vehicle Crash Information. A
Federal Register
Notice with a 60-day comment period soliciting comments on this information collection was published on June 25, 2026. NHTSA received one public comment.
DATES:
Comments must be submitted on or before November 30, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
Written comments and recommendations for the proposed information collection, including suggestions for reducing burden, should be submitted to the Office of Management and Budget at
www.reginfo.gov/public/do/PRAMain.
To find this particular information collection, select “Currently under Review—Open for Public Comment” or use the search function.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
For additional information or access to background documents, contact Liza Lemaster-Sandbank, Office of State Data Reporting System Division (NSA-0120), telephone (202) 744-5942, National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, W43-481, U.S. Department of Transportation, 1200 New Jersey Avenue SE, Washington, DC 20590. Please identify the relevant collection of information by referring to its OMB Control Number, 2127-0753.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Under the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995 (PRA) (44 U.S.C. 3501et seq.), a Federal agency must receive approval from the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) before it collects certain information from the public, and a person is not required to respond to a collection of information by a Federal agency unless the collection displays a valid OMB control number. In compliance with these requirements, this notice announces that the following information collection request will be submitted to OMB.
Title:
State Data Transfer (SDT).
OMB Control Number:
2127-0753.
Form Number(s):
N/A.
Type of Request:
Renewal with modification of a currently approved information collection.
Type of Review Requested:
Regular.
Length of Approval Requested:
Three years from date of approval.
Summary of the Collection of Information:
The State Data Transfer (SDT) program is a voluntary collection of motor vehicle crash data. Participating States electronically transfer Police Crash Report (PCR) data, supplemental crash reports, and crash images to NHTSA using automated electronic data transfer (EDT) protocols. Transfers typically occur nightly in Extensible Markup Language (XML) or JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) formats via web services. This information collection updates the burden estimates and removes the legacy State Data System (SDS) protocol, which is being sunsetted, leaving only the automated EDT protocol in place. The program includes Non-SEDC States that voluntarily transmit data under the terms of a memorandum of understanding, as well as SEDC States participating under the State Electronic Data Collection (SEDC) discretionary grant program, which requires states to modernize their crash data repositories, align with Model Minimum Uniform Crash Criteria (MMUCC) Sixth Edition standards, and transfer data electronically.
Description of the Need for the Information and Proposed Use of the Information:
NHTSA uses SDT data to identify existing and emerging highway safety trends, evaluate the effectiveness of motor vehicle safety standards, and develop countermeasures to reduce deaths and injuries from motor vehicle crashes. The data allows NHTSA to study the effectiveness of emerging technologies, such as advanced driver assistance systems (ADAS), and supplies critical volume to support cost-benefit analyses for Corporate Average Fuel Economy (CAFE) rulemakings regarding vehicle mass and fatality rates. Furthermore, automated SDT data pre-populates several NHTSA systems and special studies, including the Fatality Analysis Reporting System (FARS), Crash Report Sampling System (CRSS), and Crash Investigation Sampling System (CISS). This electronic transfer significantly reduces the administrative and technical burden on States by eliminating manual, redundant data entry into Federal databases.
60-Day Notice:
NHTSA published a 60-day notice on June 25, 2026, requesting comment on NHTSA's intention to submit this ICR to OMB for approval (91 FR 38472). During the comment period, NHTSA received one comment from Mr. Eric Hein.
Mr. Hein's comment supported the renewal of the State Data Transfer (SDT) program but was critical of how underride crashes are currently captured and transferred into NHTSA's national crash databases (such as FARS, CRSS, and CISS). He argued that underreporting and misclassification of
( printed page 68596)
underride crashes is a practical utility issue under the Paperwork Reduction Act (PRA).
